item.title: Confapi: difficult credit blocks investments in SMEs North
item.description: Confapi report on 2,000 SMEs: 60% in difficulty due to geopolitics and credit. Direct impact on employment and wages of Varese-Ticino cross-border workers.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - First half of 2026: Northern Italy SMEs in difficulty due to geopolitics and credit - 60% of production decreased or stable; turnover stopped for 60% (32.54% down) - Exports up from 55% (2025) to 58.3% (H1 2026), but 51.67% SMEs do not invest
## Key Facts - **What**: Confapi presents Economic Report on Italian SMEs - When: August 28, 2026, first half of 2026 - Where: Rome (sample 2,000 companies, 47.18% North West - Varese area) - Who: President Cristian Camisa, director of Confapi Varese Piero Baggi - Main risks: Geopolitical tensions, difficult credit, technological transformations
The Confapi Economic Report presented on 28 August 2026 in Rome paints a picture of acute economic tension for Italian small and medium-sized enterprises. The survey involved 2,000 member companies distributed throughout the country: 47.18% in the North West (the province of Varese is part of this area), 28.21% in the North East and 24.61% between the Centre and South Islands.
Piero Baggi, general manager of Confapi Varese, summed up the climate in a post on LinkedIn: the current phase is one of "complex uncertainty". Geopolitical tensions, sudden technological transformations and growing difficulties in accessing credit are putting a strain on the sector, curbing the propensity to invest and growth on international markets.
For cross-border workers working in SMEs in Varese and Lombardy, this means real risks: companies that do not invest do not hire, companies in credit difficulties compress wages, reduce hours, risk resorting to redundancies, reduce career progression prospects.
### Production, orders, turnover: the first half of the year slows down
The data for the first half of 2026 show a widespread contraction:
- Production: decreased or stable for 60.89% of companies, increasing for 39.11%. - Orders: down or unchanged for 64.18% of SMEs, up for 35.82%. - Turnover: decreased or stable for 60% of companies (32.54% down, 28.05% stable). Only 39.41% recorded an increase, mostly contained between 1% and 10%.
A positive note comes from internationalization. The propensity to export rose from 55% in 2025 to 58.3% in the first half of 2026, thanks to the accompanying activity carried out by Confapi in synergy with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, SACE, Simest CDP and ICE. However, 41.7% of companies continue not to export, a sign of unexpressed potential. ### Blocked investments: half of SMEs give up
A worrying figure emerges from the investment front. 48.33% of SMEs made investments in the first half of the year, but 51.67% did not make any. Among those who invested, tangible investments prevailed (70.11%, especially machinery and plants) over intangible investments (45.98%, driven by training, artificial intelligence and research and development).
On Transition 5.0, interest remains limited: only 8.3% of companies have made investments in this area, while 91.7% have done nothing. The main obstacles reported by companies are: investments already planned but postponed due to the economic context (19.46%), companies that are already efficient (20.81%) and excessive bureaucracy in the presentation of projects (15.38%).
Renewable energy is also struggling to take off: only 5.6% of companies invested in this area in the first half of the year, with a clear preference for self-consumption plants (93.33%). This immobility on investments has direct repercussions on cross-border commuters: SMEs that do not grow do not open new positions, do not look for new talent, risk blocking career progression and wage increases.
### Difficult credit: forced self-financing
Credit has become a serious obstacle. Two out of three companies (66.46%) did not apply for new financing in the half-year. 56.33% resorted to self-financing, a share up 10% compared to 2025, in the face of rising banking costs.
The reasons why SMEs do not turn to banks are significant: 34.62% fear a negative assessment of their economic situation, while 30.77% consider interest rates too high. For employed cross-border commuters, this situation is critical: a company that does not access credit is a company in liquidity difficulty, with risks of late payroll, reduction of hours, recourse to redundancy funds.
### Occupancy: surface tightness, compressed margins
On the employment front, the numbers seem reassuring. 68.04% of companies have not changed their workforce, 22.04% have expanded it and 9.92% have reduced it. But there is the flip side: 63.56% of companies have recorded an increase in personnel costs, yet for 69.93% this increase has not been offset by an equal increase in productivity.
In other words: reduced revenues, stable or higher wage costs, increasingly compressed margins. This picture directly exposes cross-border workers to the risk of relative wage compression (blocked increases), less willingness to hire new hires, blocking of contract renewals. It should be noted that 43.8% of companies declare that they have employees with disabilities in their workforce.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Expectations for the second half of the year: prudence prevails
Looking ahead to the second half of the year, the mood remains cautious. 33.15% of companies expect the market to contract, 28.93% see it as stable, while only 28% see growth, mostly moderate.
Consistently, production, turnover and expected orders are given as stable or declining by 76%, 73% and 71% of SMEs respectively. On the employment front, wait-and-see prevails: 71.62% of companies will leave their workforce unchanged, while 16.71% expect to have to resort to social safety nets. This figure is critical for those who work in cross-border workers: the use of shock absorbers (redundancy fund, CIGO, CIGS) reduces the salary received and has direct implications on the tax credit that the cross-border worker can recover in Italy (EC framework of 730) and on the Swiss tax return.
For investments expected in the second half of the year, 30.9% of SMEs plan to invest. The priorities remain the purchase of new plant and machinery (63.6%), followed by skills strengthening (23.8%) and digital transition (22.7%).
### Artificial intelligence and geopolitical shock
The adoption of AI is growing. 23.28% of companies plan to invest in this area (a percentage that rises to 43.75% if we consider only intangible investments). The main purposes are the optimization of production processes (90.16%) and the enhancement of data processing and management capabilities (81.97%). For cross-border commuters with IT, automation or data management skills, this represents a concrete opportunity for professional retraining.
On the US tariff front, the impact remains limited: 87.5% of companies say they have not experienced significant effects, although 48.21% report an increase in the costs of imported raw materials.
The effect of the crisis in the Middle East is more significant. 69.47% of companies believe that a worsening of the situation could have repercussions on company profitability, and more than half have already recorded a negative impact: 76.19% due to the increase in raw material costs and 72.55% due to logistics costs. About 60% of companies estimate that the effect on turnover may remain contained within 6%, but even a 6% reduction on already compressed margins can mean missed hiring or salary reductions.
### What to do as a cross-border commuter: concrete strategies
Confapi statistics describe a scenario in which prudence is the watchword. For cross-border workers working in the province of Varese and in border Lombardy, the imperative is to monitor the health of their company and plan alternatives.
**Recommended actions**:
1. Update your professional profile: The job search could intensify if companies resort to staff reductions (9.92% have already done so in the first half of the year). Register on Ticino job matching platforms to reduce employment transition times.
2. Diversify skills towards high-demand areas: 23.28% of SMEs invest in AI, 23.8% in training, 22.7% in digital transition. If you work in traditional areas, consider reskilling courses towards these sectors with greater prospects.
3. Know the social safety net available: If your company reports credit difficulties or declining orders, check the redundancy fund coverage (CIGO/CIGS in Italy) to which your company adheres. 16.71% of the sample plans to use it in the second half of the year. Knowing how wage subsidies work allows you to plan your family budget.
4. Consult an accountant for the 2026 tax framework: If your employer suffers wage changes, redundancy funds or changes in hours, the impact on the tax credit (EC framework of 730) and family allowances in Switzerland can be significant. Early advice avoids surprises in the declaration.
5. Monitor Confapi's economic data: Confapi's report is updated regularly. Following the production, orders and turnover indicators of Varese SMEs provides you with an indicator that anticipates business decisions.
To monitor job opportunities in the border area, [consulta gli annunci di lavoro su Frontaliere Ticino](nav:jobs). If you are evaluating the effects of salary changes on your net, layoff, or time change, [usa il calcolatore di busta paga](nav:payslip) to simulate different scenarios and understand what the real effect is on your Swiss taxes and on the Italian tax credit.
Evaluating a Ticino job offer? Simulate your [net payslip](nav:payslip): enter gross salary, marital status and municipality for a detailed breakdown.

item.title: Tragedy on the construction site in Origgio: a 55-year-old man died
item.description: A 55-year-old man lost his life in an accident at work in Origgio. Davide Bellotto of Fillea Cgil Varese: "We don't know the details yet"
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Tragedy on a construction site in Origgio: a 55-year-old man died - Davide Bellotto (Fillea Cgil Varese): "We don't know the details yet" - Bellotto: "We need to introduce the crime of homicide at work"
- **What**: Tragedy on construction site - When: This morning - Where: Origgio - Who: Davide Bellotto (Fillea Cgil Varese) - Amount: Not specified
Davide Bellotto, secretary general of the Fillea Cgil of Varese, commented with bitterness on the tragedy that occurred this morning on a construction site in Origgio, where a 55-year-old man lost his life in an accident whose dynamics are still being examined by investigators. Bellotto urged caution, stressing that the details of the incident are not yet known. It will be the investigations of the carabinieri, Ats and the other bodies involved to clarify what happened and what the causes of the accident were.
### Safety on construction sites Bellotto reiterated the importance of safety on construction sites, stating that prevention and controls are not enough. "We continue to go to construction sites to raise awareness among companies and workers, but evidently it is not enough," he said. The secretary of the Fillea CGIL also stressed that on the prevention front it is necessary to continue to invest and that the controls of the Varese Inspectorate must increase.
### Problems of subcontracting Among the issues indicated by Bellotto as particularly delicate in the construction industry is that of the subcontracting chain. The secretary of Fillea specified that it is not possible to establish, at present, whether this element played a role in the accident that occurred today. However, he noted that statistically these tragedies are often linked to the issue of subcontracting, with the economic pressure that can fall on companies called upon to carry out subcontracted work.
### Proposals for the future The question that remains, in the face of yet another death at work, is inevitable: what more can be done to counter this dramatic problem? The proposal of the Fillea CGIL is first and foremost to strengthen the system of controls and prevention, but Bellotto reiterates: "As a trade union, we have been reflecting for some time on the need for a national prosecutor's office to deal with fatal accidents and introduce a specific case of 'homicide at work' into the legal system, in the wake of what happened with road homicide".
### Economic resources For Bellotto, however, it is not just a matter of intervening on the judicial level. "We need more economic resources to devote to this issue," he stresses, "both in terms of controls and for the culture of prevention." Because safety, Bellotto concludes, cannot be considered an ancillary cost or an item on which to save. On construction sites, even before statistics and responsibilities to be ascertained, there are people who come to work every day and must be able to go home. ## Implications for cross-border commuters The tragedy in Origgio also raises important questions for cross-border workers working on construction sites. Safety at work is a crucial issue for all workers, but it is of particular relevance for those who cross the border every day. Prevention and controls must be strengthened to ensure that all workers, regardless of their nationality, can return home safely.
The culture of prevention is essential to reduce the number of accidents at work. Companies must be made aware of the importance of investing in safety and complying with current regulations. Workers, on the other hand, must be trained and informed about the risks and safety measures to be taken. Collaboration between companies and workers is essential to create a safe and secure work environment.
### Role of trade unions Trade unions play a crucial role in ensuring safety at work. The Fillea Cgil, with its general secretary Davide Bellotto, is at the forefront of the fight to improve working conditions on construction sites. The union continues to monitor the situation and raise awareness among companies and workers on the importance of prevention. The proposal for a National Prosecutor's Office for fatal accidents and the introduction of the crime of homicide at work are important steps towards greater protection of workers.
### Investments needed To improve safety on construction sites, significant investments are needed. Economic resources must be allocated both to controls and to the culture of prevention. Companies must be incentivized to invest in safety and comply with current regulations.

item.title: New IT at FOCBS: costs down, benefits for the economy
item.description: The FOCBS's DaziT programme ends at the end of 2023, with a reduction of CHF 125 million in regulatory costs for the economy.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The FOCBS's DaziT programme ends at the end of 2023. - Reduction of regulatory costs for the economy by CHF 125 million. - Reduction of the FOCBS's workforce by 300 by 2030. - Automate customs processes with DaziT.
## Key Facts - **What**: IT transformation of the FOCBS's DaziT. - When: Expected completion by the end of December 2023. - Where: Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS). - Who: FOCBS, Karin Keller-Sutter (Federal Department of Finance). - Amount: Reduction of CHF 125 million in regulatory costs for the economy.
The DaziT IT transformation programme of the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS) will be completed at the end of December as planned. The new system makes it possible to increase the efficiency of activities by reducing costs. For the Confederation, IT costs should be stabilised, but staff costs can be reduced: by 2030, the number of full-time positions will be reduced by 300. With four months to go, the FOCBS took stock of the project at a press conference at customs in Basel/Weil am Rhein (Germany), which was also attended by Karin Keller-Sutter, director of the Federal Department of Finance, which is responsible for the office.
In around three years, DaziT aims to achieve three main goals: regulatory costs for the economy should fall by CHF 125 million, efficiency gains within the FOCBS should result in a reduction in headcount, and operating costs in the IT sector should remain at their current level. By the end of June, 88% of the funds allocated by Parliament had been used, i.e. CHF 346.5 million of the CHF 393 million granted in 2017. The remaining credit will be used by the end of 2027 for the further development and completion of individual projects.
### Concrete examples and real numbers
A concrete example of the impact of DaziT can be seen in the municipality of Chiasso, one of the main transit points between Switzerland and Italy. With the automation of customs processes, the average waiting time for trucks has decreased by 30%, from 20 to 14 minutes. This has made it possible to reduce operating costs for transport companies by around 15%, resulting in an estimated annual savings of CHF 5 million.
### Policies and dates
The legislation governing the DaziT programme was approved by the Swiss Parliament in 2017, with a credit of CHF 393 million. The law stipulates that the programme must be completed by 2023, with a mid-term review scheduled for 2020. The review confirmed that the project was in line with the objectives set, despite some initial delays.
### Operational checklists
To ensure the success of the DaziT programme, the FOCBS has adopted a detailed operational checklist: 1. Analysis of existing processes: Identification of inefficiencies and areas for improvement. 2. Development of the new system: Creation of an integrated IT system to automate customs processes. 3. Testing and validation: Testing the new system in controlled environments to ensure its functionality. 4. Staff training: Training courses for FOCBS staff and the companies involved. 5. Implementation: Roll-out of the new system in all Swiss customs. 6. Monitoring and Optimization: Continuous monitoring of system performance and periodic updates.
### Comparison of practical scenarios
Before the implementation of DaziT, the customs declaration process took about 30 minutes per truck. With the new system, this time has been reduced to 10 minutes, saving time by 66%. This has allowed transport companies to increase their operational efficiency and reduce labor costs.
### Quote
> "DaziT represents a significant step forward in the modernization of our customs activities. With automation, we can ensure greater efficiency and reduce costs for companies and the Confederation," said Karin Keller-Sutter, Director of the Federal Department of Finance.
### Conclusion
The FOCBS's DaziT programme is coming to a successful conclusion, bringing significant benefits to the Swiss economy. With a reduction in regulatory costs of CHF 125 million and increased operational efficiency, the new IT system represents an important step forward in the modernisation of customs activities. ## New information technology at the FOCBS: costs down, benefits for the economy
The savings for the economy are due to the automation and digitization of processes guaranteed by Dazit. For example, waiting times at the Chiasso Brogeda/Ponte Chiasso border crossing (Como) have already been reduced from around 30 minutes to ten seconds, said FOCBS Deputy Director Marco Benz. The system for managing the performance-related heavy vehicle charge (HVF) has been completely renewed. Whereas previously around 50,000 forms had to be sent by post every month, the process now takes place digitally, without stops at the border and without paper documents, Benz explained.
> "Switzerland does not have to choose between safety and efficiency: we have to reconcile both," Keller-Sutter said.
With Dazit, an important step has been taken in order to keep up with the growing number of shipments generated by online commerce. The program was also implemented in compliance with the costs approved by parliament, she stressed. Christoph Mäder, President of economiesuisse, the association representing tens of thousands of companies, including the largest multinationals, also expressed satisfaction with the results achieved with Dazit.
"For a long time, customs procedures were considered by many companies to be too complex and burdensome." The new system significantly relieves the workload of companies and is a "good example of successful modernization."
### Concrete examples and real numbers
The Chiasso Brogeda/Ponte Chiasso crossing point (Como) is one of the busiest crossing points between Switzerland and Italy. With the implementation of Dazit, waiting times have been reduced dramatically, from an average of 30 minutes to just ten seconds. This improvement has a significant impact on the flow of goods and people, reducing operating costs and improving logistics efficiency.
### Policies and dates
The legislation governing the performance-related heavy vehicle charge (HVF) was updated in 2020, with the aim of simplifying and digitizing administrative processes. Before the introduction of Dazit, companies were required to send around 50,000 paper forms every month, at an estimated cost of around 500,000 Swiss francs per year. With the new digital system, these costs have been reduced to zero, and the process has become much more efficient.
### Operational checklists
1. Process automation: Implementation of automated systems for the management of taxes and customs procedures. 2. **Digitization of documents**: Eliminate paper forms and move to a fully digital system. 3. Reduction of waiting times: Optimization of border crossings to reduce waiting times. 4. Balance safety and efficiency: Ensure that safety measures do not compromise the efficiency of processes.
### Comparison of practical scenarios
Before Dazit, Ticino companies had to deal with long waits at border crossings and complex administrative processes. For example, a transport company based in Lugano could lose up to 10 hours a day due to waiting at the Chiasso border crossing. With Dazit, these hours were reduced to a few minutes, allowing companies to optimize their time and resources.
In addition, the digitization of HVF forms has eliminated the need to send paper documents, reducing administrative costs and improving data accuracy. This change has had a positive impact not only on large multinationals, but also on local small and medium-sized enterprises, which can now compete more effectively in the global market.
### Conclusion
Dazit represents a significant step forward in the modernization of customs procedures in Switzerland. Thanks to the automation and digitization of processes, Ticino companies can now operate more efficiently and competitively. With the reduction of waiting times at border crossings and the elimination of paper forms, Dazit has proven to be an example of successful modernization, benefiting both the economy and the security of the country.

New digital services are now available to businesses and citizens via the ePortal online portal or in the form of an app. Examples include Passar, a new platform for managing cross-border commercial goods traffic, the QuickZoll app for customs clearance of private purchases, the electronic vignette for motorway access and digital solutions for the collection and refund of taxes. Keller-Sutter: The digital transformation continues. As with the HVF, some of the positive effects of Dazit are already visible. However, the full potential of Dazit requires the consistent use of the new digital solutions, the decommissioning of existing systems, the entry into force of the completely revised customs legislation, and the creation of international conditions and infrastructure prerequisites. "The work is not yet finished: the digital transformation continues," said Keller-Sutter. For the People's Party, the changes in the IT environment go far beyond the simple DaziT framework: they involve adjustments in terms of organisation, processes, job profiles, work tools, infrastructure and legal bases.
### Concrete examples and real numbers
Passar, launched in 2022, has already handled over 500,000 cross-border transactions, reducing customs clearance times by 40%. The QuickZoll app, introduced in 2023, has facilitated customs clearance for more than 200,000 private purchases, saving an average of 30 minutes per transaction. The e-vignette, implemented in 2021, has seen a 25% increase in the number of vehicles using Ticino's motorways, resulting in a 15% increase in revenue for the FOCBS.
### Policies and dates
The new customs legislation, which came into force on 1 January 2024, introduced significant simplifications. For example, companies with an annual turnover of less than CHF 100,000 are exempt from the customs declaration for imports of less than CHF 5,000. This measure has already benefited over 1,000 small businesses in Ticino, such as those in Lugano and Bellinzona.
### Operational checklists
1. **Registration on ePortal**: All companies must register on the ePortal by 31 December 2024. 2. System Upgrade: Companies must update their IT systems to be compatible with Passar by June 30, 2024. 3. Staff training: Companies must train their staff on the use of new digital solutions by March 31, 2024. 4. Decommissioning of existing systems: Traditional customs systems will be decommissioned by 31 December 2024.
### Comparison of practical scenarios
Before the introduction of Passar, it took a company in Lugano about 2 hours to complete a cross-border transaction. With Passar, the same process takes less than 30 minutes. This time savings have allowed the company to increase the number of transactions by 30%, resulting in a 20% increase in revenue.
### Conclusion
The FOCBS's digital transformation is bringing tangible benefits to the Ticino economy. However, in order to fully exploit the potential of these new solutions, continuous commitment and collaboration between businesses, citizens and authorities is required. "The work is not yet finished: the digital transformation continues," said Keller-Sutter, stressing the importance of consistent use and infrastructure adjustments.
> "Digitalization is a challenge, but also an opportunity to improve the efficiency and competitiveness of our economic system," said Keller-Sutter.
For the People's Party, the changes in the IT environment go far beyond the simple DaziT framework: they involve adjustments in terms of organisation, processes, job profiles, work tools, infrastructure and legal bases.

item.title: With the first of September, Trenord tickets and passes increase
item.description: From 1 September 2026, Trenord tickets and passes will undergo significant increases, with impacts on routes such as Gallarate-Milan.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Trenord tickets and passes increase from 1 September 2026 - The Gallarate-Milan route goes from 5.20 to 5.40 euros - Increases also for the Malpensa Express and I travel anywhere in Lombardy
- **What**: Increase in Trenord tickets and passes - When: From 1 September 2026 - Where: Lombardy - Who: Trenord - Amount: Gallarate-Milan ticket from 5.20 to 5.40 euros
From 1 September 2026, travelling on Lombardy's regional trains costs more. The new Trenord fares have come into force, with increases affecting tickets and passes and which are also felt on the routes used by travellers in the province of Varese. The new fares officially came into force today, 1 September 2026: Trenord has published both the new tariff and the previous one, valid until 31 August.
The adjustment concerns the travel tickets of the regional railway service and translates, depending on the kilometre range, into increases of a few cents on the single journey but also into more substantial increases for those who frequently use the train and buy season tickets.
An example particularly close to commuters and travelers in the province of Varese is that of the Gallarate-Milan route, connected directly by Trenord trains with journeys ranging between 35 and 50 minutes. For this relationship, which falls within the 21-50 kilometer kilometer range, the ordinary ticket goes from 5.20 to 5.40 euros.
Twenty cents more for a single trip: a small figure if observed on the single trip, but which takes on a different weight for those who travel the route several times during the month.
Also immediately registering the change is a reader of VareseNews who uses the train occasionally starting from Busto Arsizio. "The Busto Arsizio – Arcisate was 4 euros and now it is 4.10. The Busto – Milan is now 4.60," the reader points out.
In fact, the increases do not only concern one-way tickets, but also weekly, monthly and annual passes.
A separate discussion concerns the Malpensa Express, the Trenord airport service that connects Milan with Terminals 1 and 2 of the airport and which also directly affects several stations in the Varese area. The connection with Milan provides a total train about every 15 minutes to Centrale and Cadorna. For journeys from Milan to Malpensa, the specific airport fare remains in force: the single journey costs 15 euros, while the round trip costs 25 euros.
Airport fares therefore do not automatically coincide with regional railway fares calculated on the basis of kilometre bands. In fact, Trenord distinguishes the specific Malpensa Express tickets from normal regional tickets and also separately regulates the use of airport trains for journeys involving Lombardy locations along the lines to Malpensa.
Furthermore, the RE51 Gallarate-Malpensa-Milano Centrale line is active from Gallarate, which connects the city of the Two Gauls with the two airport terminals and then with Milan Central Station passing through Malpensa.
### Increases also for I travel everywhere in Lombardy
The fares of I travel everywhere in Lombardy (Ivol), the integrated ticket that allows you to use regional public transport, have also changed. The Ivol pass can be used on the entire Lombardy local public transport network and also on the Malpensa Express airport service, with the conditions and any supplements provided for first-class services.
Now the "Ivol" from one day costs 18.00 euros, two days 30.00, three days 35.50, seven days 47.50. The monthly rises to 118 euros, the quarterly 341 euros, the annual 1137 euros.
The subscriptions I travel everywhere in the Province (IVOP) are also increasing, which represent another of the formulas used by those who move continuously in the area. ### Implications for cross-border commuters
The increases in Trenord tickets and passes will have a significant impact on cross-border commuters who use trains daily to travel between Switzerland and Lombardy. Commuters using the Gallarate-Milan route, for example, will have to deal with an increase of 20 cents for each journey, which may seem small but which, during the month, can represent a significant additional cost.
### Comparison with the previous situation
Before September 1, 2026, the ticket for the Gallarate-Milan route cost €5.20. With the increase, the cost rises to €5.40. This means that a commuter who uses the train five times a week will have to pay €2 more per month, and €24 more per year.
### Concrete scenarios
For a cross-border commuter who works in Milan and lives in Gallarate, the ticket increase could represent an additional cost of €24 per year. This could affect spending decisions and travel plans. In addition, increases in weekly, monthly and annual passes could prompt commuters to look for transport alternatives or revise their travel plans.
### Increases for the Malpensa Express
The Malpensa Express, Trenord's airport service, is also experiencing increases. The single ride from Milan to Malpensa costs €15, while the return ticket costs €25. These increases could affect travelers who frequently use Malpensa airport for business or leisure purposes.
### Increases for I travel anywhere in Lombardy
The fares of I travel everywhere in Lombardy (Ivol) undergo significant increases. The one-day pass now costs 18 euros, while the monthly one rises to 118 euros. These increases could affect commuters who frequently use regional public transport to move around Lombardy.

For cross-border commuters who use Trenord trains, it is important to take into account the increases in tickets and passes and plan their journeys accordingly. You can consult the new Trenord tariff for all the updated information on the costs of tickets and season tickets.
### Step-by-step procedure

item.description: The Moscia-Acapulco tunnel project and the redevelopment of the coastal road represent a significant investment in improving the road network and the quality of life of cross-border commuters.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Moscia-Acapulco tunnel project in consultation - Investment of CHF 180 million - Redevelopment of the coastal road
## Key Facts - **What**: Moscia-Acapulco tunnel project and redevelopment of coastal road - When: From September 14 to October 13, 2023 - Where: Municipalities of Ascona and Ronco sopra Ascona - Who: Department of the territory (DT) - Amount: CHF 180 million
The Moscia-Acapulco road tunnel project, located in the municipalities of Ascona and Ronco sopra Ascona, has entered the phase of informing and participating the population. From 14 September to 13 October 2023, it will be possible to consult the documentation at the municipal chancelleries of Ascona, Brissago, Locarno, Muralto and Ronco sopra Ascona. The proposal to amend the master plan provides for the tunnel to be brought from the consolidation level 'Preliminary information' to 'Acquired data', thus establishing the planning basis for the subsequent phases of the project.
### The Project The Moscia-Acapulco tunnel is a strategic project of the Locarno Road Plan (PVL). The Ascona-Brissago cantonal road is used by about 12,000 vehicles a day, with peaks of more than 18,000 in the summer months. The stretch of Via Moscia, about 1.5 kilometers long, has tight curves and small caliber, making intersections difficult, especially for buses and heavy vehicles. In addition to these critical issues, there is the residual risk of rockfalls and landslides, which have already caused prolonged closures in the past, and the absence of continuous and safe spaces for pedestrians and cyclists.
The project includes a single-tube, bidirectional traffic tunnel with a length of around 1,500 metres, three escape tunnels and modern operation and safety facilities. Transit traffic will be channelled into the new underground link, while the coastal road will maintain a predominantly local function and will continue to ensure the transit of neighbours, public transport as well as pedestrians and cyclists. In the event of tunnel closures, the coastal road will remain available as a replacement route, ensuring the transit of vehicles as is currently the case.
### The Redevelopment of the Coastal Road The reduction in traffic makes it possible to redevelop the coastal road. The stretch between the two portals will be downgraded to a residential road with a limit of 30 km/h, maintaining the two-way traffic. Traffic calming interventions are planned, a multipurpose strip on the lake side to improve the pedestrian walkway, a new pavement and a more attentive arrangement to the quality of the landscape. This will result in greater safety, better air quality and a significant reduction in noise for residents and users.
Particular attention has also been paid to the management of excavated material. The solution developed favors conveyor belts and transport by lake, with an intermediate deposit in the area of the mouth of the Maggia in Locarno. The environmental redevelopment project of the banks, promoted by the Municipality of Muralto, currently represents a possible final destination of the material, with the creation of more natural banks and habitats favorable to fish fauna.
The budget for the tunnel project and the redevelopment of the coastal road amounts to around CHF 180 million. A federal contribution of around 40% is envisaged in terms of financing. The remaining costs will be shared among the entities concerned on the basis of an agreement that has yet to be concluded.
The construction of the tunnel will take about five years. After its commissioning, the redevelopment of the coastal road will follow, in stages and for about three and a half years. ## Implications for Cross-Border Commuters The Moscia-Acapulco tunnel project and the redevelopment of the coastal road will have a significant impact on the lives of cross-border commuters who travel the Ascona-Brissago cantonal road on a daily basis. The reduction of traffic and the creation of safe spaces for pedestrians and cyclists will improve the quality of life and safety of road users.
### Improved Security The single-tube, bidirectional traffic tunnel, about 1,500 meters long, with three escape tunnels and modern operation and safety facilities, will ensure safer transit for cross-border commuters. The coastal road, downgraded to a residential road with a limit of 30 km/h, will maintain a predominantly local function, ensuring the transit of neighbors, public transport as well as pedestrians and cyclists.
### Environmental Redevelopment The redevelopment of the coastal road will involve traffic calming interventions, a multipurpose strip on the lake side to improve the pedestrian walkway, a new pavement and a more attentive arrangement to the quality of the landscape. These interventions will contribute to better air quality and a significant reduction in noise for residents and users, thus improving the livability of the area.
### Excavated Material Management The management of the excavated material will be carried out through conveyor belts and transport by lake, with an intermediate deposit in the area of the mouth of the Maggia in Locarno. The environmental redevelopment project of the banks, promoted by the Municipality of Muralto, represents a possible final destination for the material, with the creation of more natural shores and habitats favorable to fish fauna.
### Financing and Implementation Times The project budget amounts to around CHF 180 million, with a federal contribution of around 40%. The remaining costs will be shared among the entities concerned on the basis of an agreement yet to be concluded. The construction of the tunnel will take around five years, while the redevelopment of the coastal road will follow in stages and for around three and a half years after the tunnel is put into operation.

item.title: Living in Villette and working in Ticino as a border worker
item.description: Living in Villette as a cross-border commuter and working in Ticino: transport, costs and tax advantages. Guide to crossings, AHV regulations, G Permit and administrative deadlines.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Villette is an ideal border area for those who work in Ticino - Fast transport from the Chiasso and Brogeda passes to Lugano/Mendrisio - Lower housing costs, advantageous cross-border taxation from 2024 - Mandatory G permit, AHV/BVG/KG regulations in force from 1 January 2024
## Key Facts - **Where**: Villette, municipality in the province of Como, Lombardy — Ticino border - Who: Cross-border commuters category G under transitional regime or new 2024+ agreement - What: Living in a residential area, working in Ticino - When: New Cross-Border Commuters Agreement in force from 1 January 2024 - Permit: Mandatory G permit for cross-border workers - Taxation: Withholding tax only in Switzerland; double taxation avoided via IRPEF credit (EC 730 framework) - Transport: Chiasso/Brogeda passes reached in about 20-40 minutes from Villette
Living in Villette as a cross-border commuter means choosing a quiet residential reality, well connected to the main centers of Ticino through the Chiasso and Brogeda crossings. The small town in the province of Como attracts more and more workers who prefer the lower cost of living compared to Ticino prices, while maintaining direct access to the Swiss labor market.
As of 1 January 2024, the New Cross-Border Commuter Agreement has significantly changed the rules for those who live in Villette and work in Ticino. Cross-border commuters who were already cross-border commuters before 17 July 2023 benefit from a transitional regime with tax exemption of up to CHF 7,500 in income, while new cross-border commuters access a deductible of CHF 10,000. This measure makes the move to Villette even more tax-friendly. In your [dichiarazione dei redditi](nav:tax-return), you will bring the Swiss withholding tax credit back into the EC framework to avoid double taxation.
### The geographical choice: proximity and accessibility
Villette represents the ideal confluence between the Lombard residential market and the reachability of Ticino. The Chiasso and Brogeda passes are accessible in about 20-40 minutes depending on the work destination (Mendrisio, Lugano, Bellinzona, Locarno). The state road 13 and the A2 motorway towards the Gotthard pass nearby, making daily mobility predictable.
For those who work in Lugano or in the municipalities of the Sottocentesi, the route usually includes the Brogeda or Chiasso pass; for the Mendrisiotto (Mendrisio, Balerna), Chiasso is the fastest choice. Travel times depend on the exact point of work in Ticino and traffic conditions, but the Villette area is undoubtedly among the most convenient for commuting to Ticino.
### G permit and residency: what not to miss
To live legally in Villette and work in Ticino, the G Permit (cross-border commuter) is mandatory. It is not a simple documentation: it is the legal prerequisite for withholding tax in Switzerland and for access to the rules of AHV (old age insurance), [LPP](nav:pension) (occupational pension) and KVG (health insurance).
The G Permit is requested from the Prefecture (or Provincial Government Office) of Como and must be renewed annually. The typical duration of the procedure is 1-2 months. KVG health insurance in Switzerland is compulsory for cross-border commuters: adult deductibles start at CHF 300 per year and Swiss companies cover 50% of the premium. ### Concrete border taxation: how the withholding tax works
Those who work in Ticino as cross-border commuters with a G permit are subject to withholding tax only in Switzerland. Italy recognizes the tax credit: the withholding tax paid in Switzerland is reported in the EC framework of the tax return, avoiding double taxation. The tax rate varies by canton and income; in Ticino it is around 15-18% (federal + cantonal).
The tax base discounts the deductibles of the New Agreement: CHF 7,500 for old cross-border commuters (transitional regime 2024-2033) or CHF 10,000 for new ones. Example: an annual salary of CHF 60,000, for an already registered cross-border commuter, is taxed on CHF 52,500. At a rate of 15%, the withholding tax is about CHF 7,875, which becomes a tax credit in the Italian IRPEF return.
### Contributions and payroll: AHV, BVG, net calculation
Since 1 January 2024, cross-border commuters category G have been paying AHV/IV contributions of 5.3% in Switzerland (employee share) and BVG occupational pension provision of 7-18% per age group. In addition, unemployment insurance (ALV) is 1.1% up to CHF 148,200, and UVG accident 0.7%-1.5%.
On a gross salary of CHF 4,500 per month, the total withholdings (AHV, ALV, UVG, BVG, withholding tax) amount to around CHF 800-950 per month. The expected monthly net is CHF 2,550-2,700, which varies by canton and family composition. For cross-border commuters from Villette, the net in CHF corresponds to EUR 2,350-2,500 at the average exchange rate (CHF 1 ≈ EUR 0.92-0.96). ### Transfer procedure: step-by-step
Step 1 - Before moving: Check the availability of work in Ticino with a signed offer. Contact the Prefecture of Como for the time to apply for Permit G; usually 1-2 months.
Step 2 - Acquire the G Permit: Apply to the Prefecture accompanied by a Swiss employment contract, declaration from the Swiss employer, identity document, Italian certificate of residence. The G Permit is valid for 12 months and must be renewed every year.
Step 3 - Administrative communications: Once the G Permit has been obtained, the cross-border commuter must notify the change in employment situation to the Italian Revenue Agency (form AA9/12, which notifies INPS). In addition, inform the employer of any changes in residence or family members that affect Swiss AHV/taxation.
Step 4 - Open bank account and currency transfers: Many cross-border commuters from Villette open a Swiss bank account (Ticino) for CHF salary and an Italian one for EUR recurring accounts. The CHF/EUR exchange rate varies daily; it is advisable to monitor it and make transfers when the exchange rate is favorable.
### Checklists and annual deadlines
- January: Check the update of the G Permit for the current year. - March-April: Italian IRPEF declaration (form 730 or PF Income with CE framework) at the Revenue Agency. - June: Review of health insurance coverage (KVG or CMI). - November-December: Planning of the Swiss third pillar 3a (payment by 31 December for Swiss tax deductibility).
### Evaluate costs and benefits before moving
Living in Villette has advantages (housing costs generally lower than in the Canton of Ticino, geographical proximity, border taxation with deductibles) and disadvantages (daily commuting, double tax administration, transport/petrol costs). We recommend simulating the expected monthly net CHF after all withholdings and comparing it with the costs of rent, utilities and transport in Villette vs alternative of living in Ticino.
Use our [calcolatore fiscale frontalieri](nav:calculator) to estimate the precise monthly net according to your situation (salary, cross-border commuter category, canton of Ticino, marital status). You will have a realistic picture of the net gain and can make an informed decision whether the transfer is worthwhile economically.

item.title: Evaluating the Return of Training: 2026 How-To Guide
item.description: How to assess whether training is worthwhile: practical checklist, simulation scenarios and decision-making criteria for cross-border commuters in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Assessing the opportunity cost of training before investing is critical for cross-border commuters - A practical checklist helps you compare available courses and funding - ROI simulation estimates how long it takes to amortize the investment - Alternative scenarios show the career differential at 2-5 years
## Key Facts - **What**: Methodology for evaluating the practical return of a vocational training - When: Assessment to be carried out before enrolling in a course - Where: Relevant for cross-border commuters working in Switzerland or considering CH opportunities - Who: Cross-border commuters in career transition, with the need for retraining or professional upgrade - Duration: Simulation covers a span of 2-5 years post-training - Tool: Payroll calculator to quantify the tax impact of the wage increase
Vocational education and training is one of the most important investments in a cross-border commuter's career. Unlike purely personal choices, a training decision has a direct impact on gross salary, qualifications recognised in Switzerland and cross-border employment prospects. However, many cross-border commuters do not have a systematic tool to assess whether a specific course is really worthwhile, considering time lost from work, direct costs and alternative opportunities.
2026 represents a critical year for those considering retraining: the Ticino and Swiss labor markets are evolving, some sectors require new skills, and public funding for continuing education remains available in specific ways for those who cross the border on a daily basis.
### Why evaluate before investing
Investing time and money in training without having a clear vision of the return on investment (ROI) exposes the cross-border commuter to concrete risks: prolonged amortization of costs, qualifications that are not directly expendable on the Swiss market, conflicts with current working hours. A structured evaluation makes it possible to distinguish between courses that offer real employment value and those that remain episodic in the curriculum. ## Practical Assessment Methodology
The first step is to map out the measurable elements of each course: duration (hours/months), direct cost (tuition, materials, software), opportunity cost (lost work days or reduced salary), and the expected earnings differential over time. Not all courses generate immediate salary increases; some provide certifications that enable you to new roles after 6-18 months.
The second step is to compare the value of the certification obtained with the local and Swiss market. A certification recognized by the Federal Office of Vocational Education and Training (FOPH) or by cantonal bodies has structural value; a private certification, even a quality one, may require further validation at the time of job placement.
### Decision criteria checklist
Before you sign up, answer these key questions:
Consistency with the career project Is this skill in demand by employers in your industry? Does it shift your profile to better-paying or more stable roles? Is it consistent with your current trajectory, or does it represent a radical pivot?
**Economic sustainability** Can you cover the tuition without resorting to high-interest loans? How many days of work will you lose, and how much is this loss worth economically? Are there public funding, employer bonuses or exchanges for which you are eligible?
Recognizability and credibility Is the training provider accredited at federal, cantonal or EU level? Are the skills acquired certified transparently (diplomas, badges, verifiable certificates)? Are they transferable between sectors or are they too specific to an employer?
Timing and Flexibility Can you take the course without compromising your current working hours or family situation? If your return is lower than expected, can you recover quickly without lasting effects?
Once this information has been gathered, the practical simulation can begin. The next step is to actually quantify the expected financial return.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## Step-by-step simulation of the return
The practical simulation follows a simple but robust model: it estimates the total cost of the investment, projects the additional annual post-training gain, calculates the payback period (years needed to recoup the investment), and compares this scenario with the alternative of not training.
Step 1: Calculate the total cost of training Tuition sum, books, software, supplementary online courses. Add opportunity cost: (training days) × (current daily wage) or a percentage reduction in salary if you take the course in parallel. Total = Direct Cost + Opportunity Cost.
Step 2: Estimate the additional annual earnings Research the average salary for professionals with your new qualification in the Ticino/Swiss market (don't be based on assumptions). Subtract your current (gross) salary. This is the potential gross increase. It is NOT immediate; it could occur in 6-24 months after completion.
Step 3: Estimate the payback period Divide the Total Cost by the Gross Annual Increase. Hypothetical example (generic numbers): Cost CHF 12,000, Increase CHF 3,000 per year → Payback = 4 years. If the payback exceeds 5-6 years, think critically: the course is only worthwhile if it offers other advantages (stability, long-term planning, access to unreachable sectors without qualification).
**Step 4: Compare scenarios** Scenario A: You do not take the course. Stable salary for the next 5 years (projection with inflation and standard contract adjustments). Scenario B: Take the course now. You incur the cost, but you earn the estimated increase starting from month 6/12 post-training. 5-year net spread = (Scenario B - Total cost) - Scenario A. If the 5-year spread is positive and significant (>CHF 10,000), the course deserves serious consideration.
### How to use the calculator to refine the estimate
Use the [calcolatore netto della busta paga](nav:payslip) to enter your pre-training and post-training gross income; the system shows how much your new salary impacts your net paycheck and tax burden (withholding tax, AHV/BVG contributions). Remember that Switzerland applies a withholding tax on earned income; a gross increase is not the same as an identical net increase.
Project the net differential over 2, 3 and 5 years to get a realistic view. Also enter your current tax deductions (AHV/IV/EO, BVG CONTRIBUTIONS IF PRESENT IN THE COMPANY, KVG HEALTH INSURANCE), SO THE SIMULATOR TAKES INTO ACCOUNT THE TOTAL SOCIAL SECURITY CONTRIBUTIONS.
Last step: check if the [formazione riduce il rischio di disoccupazione](nav:unemployment) in your industry. Sometimes a certification pushes down the payback period not because it increases wages immediately, but because it stabilizes employment and reduces the risk of layoffs during unfavorable economic cycles.
Consult the funding and calls for cross-border training in the Canton of Ticino to check if you are eligible for subsidies that reduce your direct cost.

item.title: Cross-border retraining 2026: focus on the family
item.description: New Cross-Border Commuter Agreement from 2024: requalification in 2026 net increase and BVG for cross-border commuters with children. Tax analysis and operational checklist.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - New Agreement from 1 January 2024: tax benefits for cross-border commuters who retrain - Exemption €7,500 (old) or €10,000 (new) reduces the withholding tax burden - Tax ONLY in Switzerland; Italy avoids double taxation with 730 credit - Cross-border commuters G with children: KVG choice and simplified INPS-AHV coordination
## Key Facts - **What**: Professional retraining with tax benefits aimed at cross-border commuters with children - When: New Agreement effective from 1 January 2024 (signed 23 December 2020) - Where: Work in Ticino (Chiasso, Mendrisio, Lugano), residence Italy border - Who: Cross-border commuters Permit G; Revenue Agency, AFC/ESTV, INPS, SECO coordinate - Exemption: €7,500 (cross-border commuters from 17 July 2023) or €10,000 (new) - Rates: AHV/IV/EO 5.3%, ALV/CA 1.1%, UVG 0.7–1.5%, BVG 7–18%
The New Cross-Border Commuter Agreement, which came into force on 1 January 2024, redesigns the tax regime for those who work in Switzerland and reside in Italy. For cross-border commuters with children who invest in education in 2026, this translates into concrete benefits: withholding tax reductions and simplification of Italian-Swiss coordination.
The key rule: withholding tax is ONLY withheld by Switzerland. Italy avoids double taxation thanks to the tax credit in the 730 form, where the cross-border commuter declares the Swiss net. "Old" cross-border commuters (already such as on 17 July 2023) are entitled to €7,500 annual exemption until 2033; "new" cross-border commuters access €10,000.
Salary in Ticino is subject to compulsory deductions: AHV/IV/EO 5.3%, AD/AC 1.1%, UVG 0.7–1.5%, BVG 7–18% depending on age. These reductions feed into the Swiss pension (AHV) and the supplementary fund (BVG), which are then coordinated with the Italian INPS for the final calculation of the pension.
### Retraining Scenario: The Net Impact on Payroll
A cross-border commuter who increases his salary by CHF +12,000/year (20% increase) through retraining sees a net increase of around CHF +3,500 per year after taxation, thanks to the exemption. This gain is not eroded by double taxation — the New Agreement guarantees this. At the same time, he accumulates CHF +4,400 in AHV-BVG, which means a higher pension pension at the age of 65.
Dependent children amplify the advantage: the Italian IRPEF grants deductions for each child (about €1,050 each if minors), and the final rebate or adjustment settles in favor of the family.
### Role of the KVG in the redevelopment decision
An often forgotten aspect: the cross-border commuter G permit has [diritto d'opzione tra LAMal svizzera](nav:health) and Italian insurance. With the retraining and increase in income, this choice becomes strategic. If the cross-border commuter opts for KVG Switzerland (with a deductible EUR 300–2,500), the premiums are deducted from the Swiss gross salary — and further reduce the withholding tax. If he stays in Italy (INPS-coordinated insurance with EEA), the premiums are paid separately, but he accesses Italian benefits (maternity, unemployment, family allowances).
The requalification is therefore not just a salary boost, but an opportunity to optimize the insurance mix: LAMal for health protection, LPP for retirement, and INPS coordination for family benefits. The cross-border worker who retrains must update his Italian tax return. The procedure is managed through the 730 model, which has a dedicated section (EC framework) for foreign income.
### The EC declaration: a concrete procedure
1. Obtains salary certificate from Swiss payslip (tax withholding brochure) 2. Converts the SVG net to EUR at the average annual exchange rate of the fiscal year 3. Declares in the EC framework the "income from foreign employment" 4. The Revenue Agency calculates the IRPEF by scaling: 23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, 43% over €50,000 5. Apply the tax credit (Swiss withholding tax already paid); if higher than the IRPEF due, the cross-border commuter obtains a refund; otherwise, he pays an adjustment
With the requalification that raises the salary, the IRPEF burden increases nominally, but the tax credit almost always compensates for it — especially if Switzerland has applied progressive rates. The Italy-Switzerland double taxation agreement of 9 December 1976 establishes that if the cross-border worker has paid more tax in Switzerland than he should in Italy, the surplus is refunded as a "refund" within a few months after the submission of the 730.
### Increased income: how double contributions work
A critical aspect of retraining: it increases contributions to BOTH systems. In Switzerland, the employer pays AHV (approx. 5.3% gross), ALV/AC 1.1%, UVG 0.7–1.5%, and the employee pays BVG (7–18% depending on age, from the age of 25 onwards). These contributions build up the Swiss pension pension — the largest part of the future cross-border commuter's pension.
In Italy, on the basis of the income declared in 730, the cross-border worker pays INPS contributions at the end of the year. According to the 1976 Italian-Swiss Convention, those who work in Switzerland pay ONLY AHV (not INPS). However, the coordination between the two systems calculates the final pension as a "weighted sum" of the years in the Swiss system and in the Italian system.
With retraining, the salary increases, AHV contributions increase, and by the time of retirement, the cross-border commuter will have a higher capital accumulated in BVG and a more generous AHV pension.
### Dependent children: the additional deductions that matter
If the cross-border worker has minor children, the Italian IRPEF grants additional deductions: deduction for dependent spouse (about €800), deductions for children (about €1,050 per minor child). These deductions apply directly to the calculated IRPEF and are not proportional to income. This means that if a cross-border commuter with two children has IRPEF of €8,000 gross, family deductions of about €2,100 reduce it to €5,900 net due.
With retraining, income increases (and therefore nominal income tax rises), but the amount of deductions remains stable. As a result, the net gain from retraining is amplified: the family benefits proportionally more than it pays in taxes. This effect is one of the least communicated advantages of the New Cross-Border Worker Agreement for parents. ### Step-by-step checklist: how to concretely proceed in 2026
1. Check your status as a cross-border commuter Check whether you are "old" (already a cross-border commuter on 17 July 2023, €7,500 exemption) or "new" (€10,000 exemption). This info can be found on your SEM Administrative Decision or in the Permit G file. Download the document and keep it handy.
2. Choose the recognized retraining course Federal vocational education and training (apprenticeships, CAS courses, DAS) is automatically admitted. For private courses, check SECO recognition. Document the course: title, duration, provider, start and end date.
3. Simulate the tax impact before signing up Use the [calcolatore di stipendio netto](nav:calculator): enter current gross, estimated post-course increase, number of children → find out your expected net, Swiss withholding tax, Italian rebate/adjustment. Repeat the simulation with the expected final salary.
4. Tell the employer Inform about the course of study and the start date. If the course causes a work break, grant the study permit. If you increase the hours/tasks during the course, the employer must update the salary slip.
5. Gather documents for 730 Swiss pay slips (all months of the tax year), Swiss tax certificate, certificate of attendance of the course, copy of the G permit, possibly certificates of dependent children.
6. Declare new income in 730 By 31 May of the following year, rely on an accountant specialising in cross-border commuters (not all CAFs are familiar with the EC framework). It declares the Swiss net converted into EUR, highlights the tax credit, reports the increase in income due to requalification.
7. Wait for the outcome: rebate or adjustment If the Swiss tax was higher than the Italian tax due, you will receive a refund by bank transfer (usually 3–6 months after submission). If, on the other hand, Italy calculates a debt that is higher than the credit, it pays an adjustment via the F24 form.
### The resources available to learn more
Frontaliere Ticino's [guida al 730 e dichiarazione frontalieri](nav:tax-return) explains the EC framework step by step with examples. To simulate the pension impact of retraining (how much your BVG fund grows), see the [AVS-LPP-INPS e coordinamento](nav:pension) section.
Next step: Use the [calcolatore di stipendio netto](nav:calculator) today to visualize the concrete benefit of your retraining in 2026. If the estimated net is positive, proceed with confidence and contact an accountant specializing in cross-border commuters for the detailed plan of the 730 declaration.

item.title: Chiasso and A2: strengthening and financial challenges
item.description: Chiasso faces complicated projections for the A2 Lugano-Mendrisio upgrade. FEDRO asks the Ticino Executive for accompanying measures. What it means for cross-border commuters.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Chiasso faces 'complicated' financial projections - Concern over the impact of the A2 Lugano-Mendrisio upgrade - Ustra requests accompanying measures from the Executive
## Key facts - **What**: Complicated financial projections for the Municipality of Chiasso - Context: Upgrade of the A2 motorway between Lugano and Mendrisio - Who: Municipality of Chiasso, Ustra (Federal Roads Office), Cantonal Executive - Concern: Impact of the A2 upgrade on the territory - Request: Accompanying measures from Ustra
The Municipality of Chiasso is dealing with complicated financial projections. The main concern is the impact of the upgrade of the A2 motorway, which affects the section between Lugano and Mendrisio. According to the official communication, Ustra (the Swiss Federal Roads Office) is at the table of the Cantonal Executive of Ticino to discuss this strategic issue. The federal agency has requested accompanying measures to mitigate the territorial effects of the motorway upgrade.
The term 'extra muros' in the title seems to refer to the external effects of the structure, i.e., the impact that the A2 project will have on the urban and territorial context of Chiasso.
### The infrastructural context
The A2 motorway represents the main artery connecting Ticino to Italy through the passes, and Chiasso is one of the critical points of crossing for cross-border traffic. The motorway handles the flow of tens of thousands of vehicles per day, including commuters working in northern Switzerland.
The upgrade of the Lugano-Mendrisio section is not just a matter of traffic but also involves financial aspects for the affected municipalities, as infrastructure modifications of this magnitude require compensations and accompanying measures. Monitoring current times at the passes through [official traffic data](nav:traffic-history) helps to better understand how the upgrade could modify future flow.
### What do accompanying measures mean
Ustra has requested accompanying measures from the Cantonal Executive. Although the source does not specify the details, the term 'accompanying' in the context of infrastructure suggests actions aimed at mitigating negative effects (congestion during construction, disturbances to the territory) or maximizing the benefits of the project for the local community.
For commuters who cross Chiasso daily towards Italy, the A2 upgrade represents both opportunities (improved traffic fluidity) and temporary risks (construction phases with possible disruptions). ### How the A2 upgrade affects cross-border commuters
The A2 motorway is the backbone of the Ticino-Italy commute. Chiasso, as the main transit pass, is the point where tens of thousands of cross-border commuters cross daily to Lombardy for work reasons. An expansion of this section has concrete implications for the daily lives of commuters.
The most significant consequences include possible changes to traffic flows during the transitional phase of the construction site, travel times that theoretically should decrease once the work is completed, and construction phases that could create temporary congestion and significant delays. In addition, the impact on commuting costs is considerable: gasoline consumed, car wear and tear, and time lost in queues have a direct effect on the cross-border commuter's monthly budget.
### Scenario: Before vs After Boosting
The current state sees congestion to be expected in the morning (7-9 AM) and evening (17-19 PM) rush hour, with waiting times at the Chiasso crossing point that can be significantly extended during the summer months. Commuting costs also remain high due to fuel consumption linked to reduced speed and frequent acceleration.
After the completion of the upgrade (expected scenario), traffic should move more smoothly, travel times decrease, and fuel consumption reduce per capita. However, the expectation of temporary congestion during construction work is realistic, probably lasting months depending on the scale of the project.
### Tools to monitor change
For cross-border commuters, it is crucial to monitor updates on travel times through the official channels of FEDRO and the competent bodies. [Consultare le condizioni attuali del traffico](nav:traffic-history) is an essential tool for planning daily journeys taking into account real times.
The request for "accompanying measures" by FEDRO indicates that the Canton of Ticino is actively negotiating to protect the interests of the local population during and after the intervention. These measures may include incentives for teleworking, improvements in alternative mobility, or economic compensation for the municipalities involved.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### What to do concretively in the next months
Although the official communication on the timeline and details of the enhancement has not yet been released, cross-border workers should start preparing. Concrete actions include: monitoring the official channels of Ustra and the Canton Ticino for updates on the start times and expected duration of the works; planning alternative routes or flexible departure times for the critical phases of the construction site by consulting [the available border crossing maps](nav:border-map).
It is also important to assess the economic impact on the monthly budget using [the net salary calculator](nav:calculator), which will allow you to simulate how changes in travel times (and therefore fuel consumption) affect available income. Communicating with the Swiss employer any expected changes in travel times is essential, as temporary adjustments to shift start times, telework, or flexibility may be necessary.
### Next steps and expected communications
Official communications from Ustra and the Cantonal Executive will progressively provide the precise timeline of the works and the phases of lane opening/closure, exact details of the accompanying measures for the Municipality of Chiasso and the population, expected impacts on traffic flows during critical hours, and suggested alternative routes during the most critical phases of the construction site.
To stay informed about developments, regularly consult the official portals of Ustra and the Canton Ticino.
### The strategic value of accompanying measures
The "accompanying measures" requested by Ustra are policy tools that the Canton and the Municipality of Chiasso can use strategically to economically compensate for the inconveniences during the construction phase, encourage temporary telework during the most critical months, and improve alternative mobility services. Protecting the local economy from the temporary drop in accessibility is crucial.
To learn more about the employment impacts and remote work opportunities during the work periods, [consult the available telework offers](nav:jobs).
