item.title: Border worker dismissed 2026: notice, allowances and children
item.description: New 2024 Agreement, CO notice, INPS allowance and protections for families with children: what changes for the frontier worker
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - New Frontier Agreement in force from 1 January 2024 (not 2026) - Old border guards: exemption €7,500; new: deductible €10,000 - Tax at source only in CH, tax credit in Italy (CE framework) - Italian-Swiss double taxation agreement: 9 December 1976
## Key facts - **What**: dismissal of the border worker with family and children - When: Effective from the day of written notice - Where: Canton Ticino, employment relationship governed by the Swiss Bond Code - Who: frontier worker with G permit, Swiss employer, INPS for Italian service - Amount: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% employee; AD/AC 1.1% up to CHF 148'200; LPP 7-18% by age group from 25 years - Reference: Italy-Switzerland Convention of 9 December 1976; New Agreement of 23 December 2020, ratified by Law 83/2023 - Income tax rates: 23% up to €28,000; 35% between €28,001 and €50,000; 43% over €50,000
A frontier worker who falls into the category of "old frontier workers" — already such before 17 July 2023 — continues to benefit from the exemption of €7,500 and the transitional regime 2024-2033. For new frontier workers, on the other hand, the deductible rises to €10,000. The tax at source is withheld exclusively in Switzerland, while in Italy the tax credit mechanism to be indicated in the EC framework of 730 is applied, thus avoiding double taxation.
### The regulatory framework between Switzerland and Italy Taxation When the termination letter arrives, the first practical effect for a cross-border worker concerns the notice period: the Swiss Code of Obligations provides for increasing notice periods based on years of service. During the notice period, the employment relationship continues regularly, with a Swiss paycheck, AVS/AI/IPG contributions, AD/AC, LPP and source tax withholding. LAINF coverage remains active. The worker continues to be registered in Switzerland with a G permit and maintains their tax domicile in Italy.
### What happens at the end of the employment relationship Upon termination, the Swiss employer issues the work certificate and transmits the data to the AVS compensation fund and the cantonal tax office. The cross-border worker retains the G permit for a limited period, but validity is tied to the existence of an employment relationship or lucrative activity. For new cross-border workers hired after July 17, 2023, a deductible of €10,000 applies; for existing cross-border workers, the exemption of €7,500 remains with the transitional regime expiring in 2033. Swiss source tax is calculated on the entire dependent employment income: Switzerland withholds at source, Italy avoids double taxation with a tax credit (section CE of the 730 form).
### Hypothetical scenario: family with children A cross-border worker with a G permit, married with dependent children, in a similar situation should consider three key aspects. First: the notice period according to the Code of Obligations and the individual contract conditions; during the notice period, taxable income in Switzerland remains subject to source tax at cantonal rates, while in Italy the tax credit applies. Second: the Italian contribution position, which requires continuation of the INPS position through credited contributions or a benefits claim. Third: health coverage. LAMal is Swiss health insurance (not a health tax): cross-border workers with a G permit have the option to choose between Swiss insurance with the possibility of adult deductibles from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 and equivalent Italian coverage. The decision must be communicated within the deadlines set by the relevant health insurance fund.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). Upon receipt of the termination letter, the first concrete step is to verify the receipt date, which sets the notice period. The next step is to request from the employer the letter with the reason for termination, the calculation of the notice period, and confirmation of the last working day. The third step concerns the payslip: verify that the deductions AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%, AD/AC 1.1% up to the cap of CHF 148,200 and LPP are correct, and that the work certificate is issued upon termination. The AVS compensation fund receives contributions until the last month of work; beyond that date, the Italian contribution position follows INPS rules.
### Step-by-step procedure for a cross-border worker with family Step 1 — Keep all documentation: contract, termination letter, pay slips from the last twelve months, work certificate. Step 2 — Verify your fiscal category: old cross-border worker (exemption €7,500, transitional regime 2024-2033) or new cross-border worker (allowance €10,000). Step 3 — Submit your income tax return in Italy with section CE for the tax credit, thus avoiding the double taxation provided for by the Convention of 9 December 1976. Step 4 — Evaluate health coverage: with permit G you have the right of choice between LAMal and the Italian system; the adult deductible varies from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500. Step 5 — If you have dependent children, update your family situation with the Tax Agency for IRPEF deductions and with the health insurance company for any transition to a lower premium. Step 6 — Consult a tax consultant specializing in Italian-Swiss taxation for the INPS contribution position and for the income tax return in the year of termination.
To simulate the impact of termination on net pay and withholding tax, use the [salary calculator for cross-border workers](nav:calculator). To estimate the CHF/EUR exchange rate for any severance payments, the [currency comparator](nav:exchange) is the dedicated tool. For health coverage after the end of the employment relationship, the guide [LAMal for cross-border workers](nav:health) clarifies rights of choice and deductibles. For those seeking a new position in Canton Ticino, [job listings for cross-border workers](nav:jobs) are filtered by sector and experience level. For an overview of permits G and B, the [permit comparator](nav:permit-compare) compares living and working conditions. For information on [unemployment benefits for cross-border workers](nav:unemployment), the specific guide clarifies access conditions and coordination with INPS.

item.title: Home crisis in Como: 1,302 vacant homes, young people on the run
item.description: In July 2025, the province of Como had 1,302 vacant public accommodations. Unions denounce: workers and young people do not find sustainable homes. Housing costs push some into the Swiss labour market.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - In July 2025: 1,302 vacant public housing units in the Province of Como - Companies are looking for over 4,100 workers but struggle to find them for one in two roles - Housing costs are pushing some toward the Swiss labor market
- **What**: Housing crisis in the Province of Como with effects on the ability to attract workers - When: July 2025 - Where: Province of Como, border area with Switzerland - Who: CGIL Como, CISL dei Laghi, UIL del Lario, ALER, Municipalities - Vacant housing: 1,302 public housing units (611 owned by ALER, 691 by the Municipalities) - Planned hires: 4,100+ entries in July, 11,800 in the July-September quarter - Recruitment difficulties: for one in two roles, according to Excelsior UnionCamere
In July 2025, the Province of Como counted 1,302 vacant public housing units: 611 owned by ALER and 691 by the Municipalities. A scenario that the unions consider emblematic of a housing crisis that no longer concerns only those experiencing fragility, but also workers, young people, and families with ordinary incomes. CGIL Como, CISL dei Laghi, and UIL del Lario have decided to bring the issue of housing to the Provincial Competitiveness Table, recognizing that the cost of living is now a decisive issue for the territorial future.
The paradox is evident in the labor market figures. In July 2025, companies in the Como area planned over 4,100 new entries and almost 11,800 in the July-September quarter. Yet, according to Excelsior UnionCamere, for one in two roles companies expect recruitment difficulties. The question that emerges is urgent: can we discuss the shortage of workers without asking ourselves whether those workers can afford to live here? How is it possible that the area is looking for personnel and at the same time fails to offer affordable housing conditions?
### Housing wealth that becomes a constraint
Como is an attractive territory. Property values remain sustained by the strength of the lake, international tourism, proximity to Switzerland, and significant foreign demand. But this wealth produces effects that need to be managed: the cost of living weighs more and more on ordinary incomes. It no longer concerns only those who access public housing. There is an ever-widening segment of workers and families who do not meet the requirements for public housing but struggle enormously to sustain private market prices. The studies by Professor Giancarlo Blangiardo on the demographic prospects of the Lake Como area have already drawn attention to the reduction of the working-age population in the coming years. The problem is not remote: it has consequences today. It prevents young people from staying, discourages relocations for work, complicates the choices of those considering a competition for essential public services. ### The phenomenon of the exodus towards Switzerland
The province of Como is a border territory. In this geographical context, faced with such high housing costs, some people can look towards the Swiss labour market. It is a rational choice: sustaining ever-higher rents is, for many, well worth working abroad. The regional unions do not say it directly, but the message is clear in their statement: if you do not concretely tackle the housing crisis, do not even try to retain the workers you manage to find.
The issue concerns both those already residing in Como and those considering a move for work. There are young people deciding whether to stay or leave, those weighing geographical mobility, those who must choose whether to take part in a competition for essential public services. A rent that absorbs 40%, 50% or more of net income makes living in Italy progressively less convenient compared to a Swiss salary, even taking into account the different tax conditions and the cost of living in the two countries. The province thus loses human capital, skills, and energy. [Discover job opportunities in the province](nav:jobs).
### Public and private workers, and territorial competitiveness
Initiatives in the meantime have not been lacking. Regione Lombardia, municipalities, ALER, cooperatives, the Prefecture, economic organisations and the Third Sector have promoted interventions and projects. But the crux, according to the unions, is to turn these resources into a coherent strategy. Governance is needed that can align different resources in the same direction, create critical mass, and move from responding to today's needs to planning for the coming years.
This is not just a welfare issue. It is a matter of economic development and territorial attractiveness. If a company cannot find staff, if a public service struggles to attract professionals, if a young person leaves because rent absorbs too much of their income, housing also becomes a competitiveness problem. A competitive territory is not only one that attracts capital and businesses: it is one that manages to retain people, allowing those who work to live, put down roots and build their own future.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Resources already available: ALER, Municipalities and social housing
The province is not starting from scratch in its attempt to solve the crisis. As of July 2025, 1,302 public housing units were already available for recovery: 611 owned by ALER and 691 by the Municipalities. On top of these, there is cooperative housing stock, social housing programmes and new resources made available by Regione Lombardia. These latest regional social housing initiatives aim to provide a response precisely for that segment of workers and families who do not meet the requirements for public housing but struggle to keep up with market prices.
To search for a home in Como through ALER, you can contact the agency directly to find out about housing availability in the municipality where you wish to live. The Municipalities of the province directly manage 691 housing units: get in touch with the public residential housing office of the Municipality you are interested in. Regione Lombardia has also promoted social housing interventions specifically targeted at this segment of the population.
CGIL Como, CISL dei Laghi and UIL del Lario propose bringing housing, employment and territorial attractiveness to the Provincial Competitiveness Table. What is being asked is not a new table, but the use of an existing one, specifically set up to bring together trade unions, businesses, institutions and local stakeholders. This body should build consensus among different interests on strategic choices.
The goal is to turn what today remains a fragmented response to needs into a comprehensive strategy: recovering vacant properties, increasing supply at affordable costs, making full use of available resources and building responses for those who come to Como to work must all become parts of the same territorial development policy.
### From management to planning
The province of Como must decide whether to keep chasing emergencies or try to anticipate change. For those weighing up whether to work in Como or move to Switzerland, the cost of housing remains a decisive factor. A strategy that solves the housing problem is not just a matter of humanitarian concern: it is an economic development choice that directly affects the competitiveness of the province.
If you are considering the Swiss job market for reasons related to housing costs, compare your options. [Calculate your net cross-border commuter income](nav:calculator) and [compare the cost of living between Como and Ticino](nav:cost-of-living) to make an informed decision. The new 2024 cross-border commuter tax agreement has changed some conditions: assess whether the tax rates and fiscal benefits make moving worthwhile.
*Source: [comozero.it](https://comozero.it/attualita/provincia-di-como-sempre-meno-case-per-lavoratori-giovani-e-famiglie-sono-1302-gli-alloggi-sfitti/)*

item.title: Trenord, 3.88% increase on lines with Ticino
item.description: From 1 September, tickets and Trenord subscriptions are 3.88% more expensive: an increase ordered by the Lombardy Regional Government, with exceptions for Malpensa Express and Como-Malpensa via Chiasso and Mendrisio.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Trenord: 3.88% price increase from Tuesday, September 1st - The increase also affects cross-border lines with Canton Ticino - Malpensa Express and Como-Malpensa via Chiasso and Mendrisio: prices unchanged - Decision taken by the Lombardy Regional Council
- **What**: 3.88% price increase on tickets and season tickets of the Trenord regional rail service - When: from Tuesday, September 1st - Where: Trenord regional lines, including cross-border lines with Canton Ticino - Who: Lombardy Regional Council (decision); Trenord (operator); unions and commuter associations (protesting) - Cause 1: adjustment to the average of two Istat indices - Cost of living index (April 2025 – April 2026): 2.6% - Transport sector index: 3.9% - Exceptions: Malpensa Express (tariff frozen until September 1st, 2027); Como-Malpensa connection via Chiasso and Mendrisio (price unchanged) - Reactions: unions and commuter associations criticize the price increase, contesting the quality of the service
From Tuesday, September 1st, travelling with Trenord costs more. The decision was taken by the Lombardy Regional Council, which ordered a 3.88% increase applied to tickets and season tickets of the regional rail service. The measure, as reported by the Ticino daily newspaper La Regione, also affects the cross-border lines connecting Lombardy to Canton Ticino, that is, the rail connections used daily by commuters and cross-border workers who return to Italy after work or, conversely, reach Swiss territory.
### How the 3.88% was reached
The increase is not an isolated initiative by Trenord, but stems from a mechanism introduced with the reform of the regional transport law, which effectively makes it automatic. The price increase indeed derives from the average of two Istat indicators: the cost of living index between April 2025 and April 2026, equal to 2.6%, and the transport sector index, equal to 3.9%. Added to these is the assessment (positive or negative) on the achievement of the performance targets set in the service contracts with transport companies.
### The exceptions to the tariff
Not the entire Trenord network will undergo the increase. The Malpensa Express tariff — the dedicated connection between Milano Centrale and Malpensa airport — remains frozen until September 1st, 2027. The price of the ticket for the Como-Malpensa connection via Chiasso and Mendrisio is also unchanged, a route that crosses the border twice and represents a transport option for those travelling between the eastern strip of Canton Ticino and the Como area or the airport.
### The front of discontent
The news of the price increase was received negatively by unions and commuter associations, which contest the quality of the regional rail service. The criticisms, as reported by La Regione, focus on the relationship between the rising cost of travel tickets and the reliability of trains, an issue that in recent months has cyclically returned to the centre of the debate on Lombardy rail infrastructure, particularly on the routes with the highest commuter traffic density. ### What changes for those travelling between Lombardy and Canton Ticino
The 3.88% increase also explicitly applies to the cross-border lines with Canton Ticino — an important clarification for cross-border workers who return to Italy every day — or several times a week — from stations in Ticino, as well as for Italian commuters who work at companies situated beyond the border. For these people, the ticket or season ticket represents a fixed cost item, on which the new regional fare is now applied.
The fact that the decision was formalised by the Lombard regional government, and not by Trenord on its own, signals that the mechanism is of a political-administrative nature: the increase is tied to national statistical indices (Istat) and to contractual performance targets. In practice, the end user — whether a cross-border worker or a commuter — cannot intervene in determining the fare increase, but can evaluate their own mobility options in light of the exceptions provided.
### Who is NOT affected by the increase
There are two cases in which the fare remains unchanged. The first is the Malpensa Express, the service dedicated to Malpensa Airport, whose price is frozen until 1 September 2027. The second is the Como–Malpensa connection via Chiasso and Mendrisio, a route that — crossing the Chiasso border and the Mendrisio hub — links the Lake Como area with the airport hub passing through Canton Ticino. For those who regularly use this route, therefore, the expense item remains unchanged compared with the previous period.
### A dispute that also concerns cross-border traffic
The protest from unions and commuter associations fits into a context of growing dissatisfaction with the price/quality ratio of the regional rail service. The most critical issues — delays, cancellations, overcrowding during peak hours — also directly affect travellers moving between Lombardy and Canton Ticino, particularly on the lines that converge towards the border points of Chiasso and Lavena-Ponte Tresa. For a cross-border worker who takes the train every morning to reach their workplace, the 3.88% increase is therefore added to a service picture that the trade associations themselves consider unsatisfactory.
### A look at the calendar
The increase comes into force precisely on 1 September, coinciding with the full resumption of work and school activities after the summer break. For cross-border workers returning from their holidays and for commuters resuming their routine after the summer, the first renewed ticket or season ticket will therefore already be calculated at the new fare. The date of 1 September 2027 — the end of the Malpensa Express freeze — instead represents a long-term time reference, useful for those planning regular trips to Malpensa Airport over the next twelve months.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### What to do, concretely
For a cross-border commuter using Trenord lines on the cross-border routes with Canton Ticino, the first step is to check on which routes the 3.88% fare increase actually applies and on which, instead, the exceptions apply. The Malpensa Express and the Como-Malpensa connection via Chiasso and Mendrisio — as reported by La Regione — are not subject to any price changes.
Anyone who holds an annual or monthly Trenord pass can already check on their profile (on the app or on the Trenord website) the renewal date and the updated amount. For single tickets purchased at the ticket machines or at the ticket office, the new price will be automatically applied starting from 1 September. It is advisable to keep the receipts of purchases made close to the date the fare increase comes into force, in case it is necessary to report an abnormal charge.
### Reporting service disruptions
Unions and commuter associations have announced their opposition to the fare increase, contesting the quality of the service. Travellers can help document service disruptions by using the official Trenord channels (app, website, contact centre) and reporting delays, cancellations or overcrowding. Trade associations collect the reports to support their claims with the Region and the operator.
### Travelling to Malpensa
For those using the Malpensa Express to reach the airport, the fare remains unchanged until 1 September 2027: no price changes are expected on this route over the next year. For the Como-Malpensa connection via Chiasso and Mendrisio, the ticket price remains the same as before, with no freeze deadlines communicated.
### Useful tools
For those who need to reorganise their daily travel between Italy and Canton Ticino, it is useful to consult the page dedicated to [public transport in Ticino](nav:transport), with up-to-date timetables and routes. For those who prefer to travel by car, the section on [waiting times at the border crossings](nav:border) allows you to monitor traffic at Chiasso, Brogeda and Ponte Tresa. The [net salary calculator for cross-border commuters](nav:calculator) remains available to simulate the impact of transport costs on the monthly pay slip.

item.title: LPP fee: minimum rate increase to 1.75%
item.description: The Federal Commission on Occupational Welfare is asking for an increase from 1.25% to 1.75%. Decision to the Federal Council. Direct impact for border workers working in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - LPP Commission requests increase of minimum rate from 1.25% to 1.75% - 0.5 percentage point increase on mandatory pension funds - Positive financial markets in 2025 and 2026 the basis for the request - Final decision rests with the Swiss Federal Council
## Key facts - **What**: Increase of minimum interest rate under the second pillar (LPP) - Institution: Federal Commission for Occupational Pensions - Percentages: From 1.25% to 1.75% (increase of 0.5 points) - Period: Positive markets in 2025 and so far in 2026 - Final decision: Swiss Federal Council - Commission votes: 10 in favour, 4 against
The Federal Commission for Occupational Pensions (LPP Commission) has recommended to the Federal Council to raise the minimum interest rate on second-pillar assets from 1.25% to 1.75%. An increase of 0.5 percentage points that directly affects the pension savings of every Italian cross-border worker employed in Switzerland.
### Legal parameters and market situation
According to the law on occupational pensions, the LPP Commission recalls in a released note, the parameters for this decision are the yield of Confederation bonds and the performance of stocks, bonds and real estate on the financial markets. In 2025 and so far in 2026, the markets have recorded a positive performance, a central element in the Commission's recommendation.
But the assessment did not stop at market data alone. The Commission also considered the overall financial situation of pension institutions, the evolution of wages in the country, inflation trends (rising prices), the actual returns achieved by pension institutions in previous years, the current interest rate policy and the estimated theoretical return of pension funds.
### The 'overall positive' situation and residual risks
In light of this 'overall positive' financial situation, the LPP Commission argues, the rate should be increased. However, the federal body did not ignore the uncertainties and risks present in the global economic scenario, particularly the geopolitical risks that continue to characterise international markets.
The decision to recommend the increase was taken with 10 votes in favour against 4, indicating a solid majority within the Commission, although a significant minority opposed it. [The LPP minimum interest rate](nav:pension) represents a crucial legal guarantee for those working in Switzerland: it is the minimum return that employers must credit annually to their employees' pension funds, regardless of market performance. ### What the increase from 1.25% to 1.75% means for your retirement capital
The minimum interest rate under the LPP is not a variable market return, but a fixed legal guarantee. Every year your employer must credit to your individual retirement account a minimum percentage of interest on all contributions paid and on previously accumulated interest. Until now this minimum was 1.25%. If the Federal Council approves the Commission's recommendation, the new minimum will rise to 1.75%.
On paper, an increase of 0.5 percentage points may seem marginal. But when you calculate the compound effect over long periods—remember that the LPP is built on the logic of long-term accumulation, typically 30–40 years of working career—the difference becomes significant. Every year the new rate applies both to your paid contributions and to the interest already accumulated, creating an exponential growth effect.
A cross-border worker who accumulates capital in the second pillar over three decades will feel this percentage difference in the final capital available at retirement. It is not a huge figure, but it provides greater protection for your future purchasing power.
### The role of the LPP Commission and how the decision-making process works
The Federal Commission for Occupational Pensions is not a political body, but an independent technical body. Its task is to formulate annual recommendations based on objective economic indicators: the return on Confederation bonds, the performance of equity markets and real estate markets. It is not a discretionary choice, but an assessment of data.
Its recommendation of 1.75% is now awaiting the formal decision of the Federal Council. Officially, the Federal Council is not obliged to follow the Commission's recommendation, although in practice it almost always does when the market context is clear and converging, as in this case with the positive markets in 2025 and 2026.
### Implications for those working cross-border between Ticino and Italy
If the new rate is approved, the effect is universal and non-discriminatory: it applies to all Swiss pension institutions subject to the Occupational Pensions Act (LPP), regardless of the employee's nationality. If you are an Italian cross-border worker residing in Ticino or in the Lombardy border area and you work for a Swiss company, the new guaranteed minimum rate applies to you just like any other Swiss worker.
Your [payslip](nav:payslip) you receive in Switzerland includes the employer's contributions to the LPP (typically between 7% and 18% of gross salary depending on age). A higher minimum rate on these funds protects your capital from any years of downturn in the financial markets and guarantees a predefined, secure growth.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to monitor the decision of the Federal Council
The ball is now in the hands of the Federal Council. The LPP Commission has made its recommendation, but there is no official public deadline communicated in the source for the final decision. Typically these decisions are made in the autumn months, but you can expect the Federal Council to officially communicate the result via Swiss federal institutional channels.
As a border worker, the concrete steps you can take are:
1. Consult the website of the Secretariat of State for the Economy (SECO), where official communications on occupational pension decisions are published 2. Contact your employer or LPP fund administrator to ask when they will communicate the new rate to employees and how it will be implemented 3. Request the annual statement of your pension fund to verify the interest credited year by year 4. If you are in complex situations (more funds, changes of company, repatriation of funds to Italy), consult a tax advisor specialized in border matters
### Tools to calculate the impact on your future income
Use the [calcolatore della pensione](nav:pension) on our website to concretely estimate how the increase in the minimum interest rate affects your final capital at the time of retirement. Enter your gross annual contribution paid to the LPP, your current age and the number of years
*Source: [swissinfo.ch](https://www.swissinfo.ch/ita/commissione-lpp%3a-aumentare-il-tasso-d%27interesse-minimo-di-0%2c5-punti/91982518)*

item.title: Living in Cirimido, working in Ticino: border guide
item.description: Find out how to move to Cirimido and work in Ticino as a border worker: G Permit, tax at source, AVS/LPP, cost of living, border crossings.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Cirimido is located just 1–7 km from the border crossings towards Ticino (Brogeda, Gaggiolo) - A Permit G is required to work in Ticino, mandatory for cross-border workers - Withholding tax is retained in Switzerland; double taxation is avoided through the Convention - New Agreement (effective January 1, 2024): €10,000 exemption (new) or €7,500 (existing)
## Key Facts - **What**: Living as a cross-border worker in Cirimido and working in Canton Ticino - Where: Cirimido (Lombardy, Como) borders Ticino; border crossings Brogeda, Gaggiolo, Chiasso, Ponte Tresa - Permit: Permit G (cross-border workers) mandatory, renewable annually - Taxation: Withholding tax retained only in Switzerland; tax credit in Italy - Agreement: New Cross-Border Workers Agreement signed December 23, 2020, effective January 1, 2024 - Rates: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% (employee), LPP 7–18% per age bracket (from age 25), LAMal exemption CHF 300–2500
Cirimido offers an interesting opportunity for those who want to work in Switzerland while maintaining Italian cost of living. Just a few kilometers from the border with Canton Ticino, this Lombard municipality is home to thousands of cross-border workers who cross into Mendrisio, Lugano, Bellinzona, and other Ticino cities every day. The economic advantage is real — housing, fuel, and food cost less than in Ticino — but this choice requires administrative preparation and a clear understanding of tax and social security regulations. This article explains how to live and work as a cross-border worker in Cirimido, what makes sense, what it costs, which documents you need, and how to navigate the Swiss-Italian system.
### Strategic location: border crossings Cirimido is just a few kilometers from Switzerland. The Brogeda crossing is the closest, about 1 kilometer as the crow flies. Gaggiolo, the second main access point, is about 7 kilometers away. For those working in southern Ticino (Mendrisio, Lugano), Brogeda and Gaggiolo are optimal choices. Those with employment further north (Bellinzona, Locarno, Ascona) will use Chiasso (about 20 kilometers) or Ponte Tresa (about 15 kilometers). This variety of crossings allows the cross-border worker to choose based on the employer's location. The advantage is clear: less time behind the wheel, lower mobility costs, less commute stress.
### Permit G: the mandatory document To legally work in Switzerland as an Italian resident, every cross-border worker must have a Permit G (Grenzgängerausweis). It is not optional: without it, it is not possible to carry out regular dependent work in Swiss territory. Permit G is tied to the employment contract and is issued by Canton Ticino. The procedure is straightforward but requires coordination: the Swiss employer submits the application to the Ticino migration authorities (SEM — State Secretariat for Migration, on behalf of the canton). Processing takes approximately 3–4 weeks. Once approved, the permit is valid for 12 months with automatic renewal as long as the employment contract persists and the cross-border worker does not violate Swiss law. To better understand the tax system that affects your net salary, you can use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) from Frontaliere Ticino.
### Immediate economic advantages Those who choose Cirimido significantly reduce their cost of living compared to Ticino. Real estate, groceries, fuel, and services (hairdresser, gym, dining) cost less in Lombardy. Furthermore, salary is paid in CHF (Swiss franc), a currency stronger than EUR, which further increases purchasing power in Italy. A cross-border worker earning CHF 50,000 annually enjoys a more favorable economic situation than a Ticino employee with the same amount in CHF spent directly in Ticino, especially considering the cost of living in Switzerland compared to Italy. ### Taxation: the Italy-Switzerland border worker system Taxation of border workers is governed by two main agreements: the Convention between Italy and Switzerland, signed on December 9, 1976, which prevents double taxation; and the New Border Worker Agreement, signed on December 23, 2020 and entering into force on January 1, 2024, which has modernized the taxation regime. The cardinal principle is that the tax on the source of labor income is withheld solely in Switzerland, never in Italy. On the border worker's Swiss pay slip, a line item for "Source tax" withheld by the employer will appear. In Italy, double taxation is avoided through a tax credit: in the Italian tax return (model 730 for employees or Redditi for self-employed), the Swiss income is entered in schedule CE, and the Italian tax authority recognizes a credit for taxes paid in Switzerland, normally resulting in a refund.
### Exemptions: how tax charges change The New Agreement established two different regimes depending on the employment start date: - **Former border workers** (already in status before July 17, 2023): exemption of €7,500 on annual gross taxable income, with transitional regime valid until the end of 2033. - New border workers (hired from July 17, 2023 onwards): exemption of €10,000 on annual gross taxable income, permanent.
The exemption reduces the amount on which to calculate the Swiss source tax. Example: a new border worker with annual gross income of CHF 60,000 deducts CHF 10,000, leaving CHF 50,000 taxable in Switzerland. The source tax is calculated on CHF 50,000, not CHF 60,000.
### Social Security: AHV, IV, BVG, unemployment Border workers are obligated to contribute to the Swiss social security system. The contribution rates on salaries (employee portion) are: - AHV/IV/EPI (pensions/disability/earnings supplement): 5.3% - Unemployment insurance (with upper income limit of CHF 148,200): 1.1% - Accident insurance (SUVA): 0.7–1.5% - BVG (occupational pension fund, second pillar): 7–18% depending on age bracket from age 25 onwards
AHV is mandatory insurance that contributes to an independent Swiss pension annuity separate from the Italian INPS pension. BVG is the occupational pension fund: the employer contributes one portion, the employee another. Those wishing to deepen their understanding of pension building can consult the [guide on AHV and BVG](nav:pension).
### KVG: Health Insurance KVG (Krankenversicherung, health insurance) is mandatory in Switzerland. Border workers have an option: they can sign up for Swiss KVG or maintain Italian health insurance. If they choose Swiss KVG, they pay a monthly premium with a deductible ranging from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 annually depending on the chosen coverage level. The decision must be made within 3 months of starting employment. Many border workers maintain Italian coverage to simplify compliance. For a personalized assessment, consult the [KVG/CMI section](nav:health).
### Tax Refunds: recovering taxes paid in excess If the Swiss source tax was higher than what was owed (because the border worker benefited from deductions, tax brackets, or credits not applied at source), it is possible to request a refund from the Swiss Federal Tax Administration (FTA). In Italy, the 730 provides the tax credit automatically. Combined, refunds from Switzerland and Italy can amount to significant sums — up to several thousand CHF for high-income border workers. To better calculate possible refunds, the site provides a [detailed guide to refunds](nav:ristorni).
### Double Taxation: how the Italian tax credit works The Italy-Switzerland convention of December 9, 1976 prevents the payment of labor income tax in both Switzerland and Italy. If the border worker pays tax in Switzerland (via source withholding), in Italy the tax authority recognizes a tax credit in model 730. The credit is normally equal to the foreign tax paid, up to the amount of Italian tax owed. In practice, most border workers receive a net refund in Italy because the Swiss tax is lower than the Italian tax on the same amount.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Checklist: practical preparation for relocation
Before relocating to Cirimido as a cross-border worker, it is essential to complete a series of formalities. Here is the recommended order:
1. Sign an employment contract in Switzerland The first step is to find an employer in Ticino (or elsewhere in Switzerland) and obtain a written job offer. Without it, Permit G is not issued.
2. Request Permit G through your employer The Swiss employer fills out the application form and sends it to Canton Ticino (SEM). Processing takes 3–4 weeks. Once approved, the cross-border worker receives the document valid for 12 months, automatically renewable.
3. Notify INPS of the start of employment INPS must be informed of the start of employment in Switzerland. This notification is important to avoid contribution penalties and to ensure that Swiss contributions are properly tracked in the Italian social security system.
4. **Choose health coverage** Within 3 months of hiring, the cross-border worker decides whether to subscribe to Swiss LAMal or maintain Italian health insurance. If choosing LAMal, they request enrollment through their employer. If remaining with Italian insurance, they communicate the new address to their current insurer.
5. Open a bank account (optional but recommended) Many cross-border workers maintain Italian accounts and exchange CHF/EUR through banks or online services (costs and rates vary). Others open Swiss accounts to receive payment directly in CHF. Check exchange commissions and account maintenance fees.
6. Prepare tax documentation Keep all Swiss tax documentation from your employer (tax certificate, Quittung or equivalent). It is essential for completing the Italian 730 tax return with the tax credit in section CE.
### Procedure: annual tax declaration Each year, the cross-border worker must declare Swiss income in Italy using form 730 (employees) or Income Models (self-employed). In the 730 form, gross Swiss income is entered in section CE as "foreign employment income". Italian tax authorities calculate the tax owed and recognize the tax credit for Swiss tax paid at source. In most cases, the cross-border worker receives an overall refund (the amount of Italian tax owed is less than what was already paid in Switzerland). The declaration must be submitted within the required deadlines (usually by May/June for form 730, by November for Income Models).
### AVS and LPP: how pension pillars work AVS contributions (Old-age, Survivors and Disability Insurance) are mandatory in Switzerland and contribute to a Swiss pension annuity independent of the Italian INPS pension. When the cross-border worker reaches age 65 (men) or 64 (women), or meets contribution criteria, they receive a Swiss AVS annuity based on average wages paid and contribution duration. It is not cumulative with Italian INPS — the two systems remain separate. LPP (Occupational Pension Fund, Swiss second pillar) is the occupational pension fund. It becomes mandatory from age 25 if the annual salary exceeds a minimum threshold. The cross-border worker and employer pay contributions proportional to the age bracket: 7–18% of coordinated salary. Upon termination of employment, the accumulated LPP can be withdrawn in full (as capital) or kept tied up in a custody account (Leistungskonto) for possible future use (home purchase, transfer to new employment).
### Scenario: how the New Agreement applies to cross-border workers Let's imagine a new cross-border worker (hired in 2024) residing in Cirimido and working in Ticino. Annual gross salary: CHF 60,000. Exemption: CHF 10,000. Swiss taxable income: CHF 50,000. Tax at source (federal + Ticino cantonal rate, usually 13–16% combined): approximately CHF 6,500–8,000. AVS/AI/IPG (5.3% of CHF 60,000): CHF 3,180. LPP (example 8%, employee portion): CHF 4,000. Approximate net: CHF 45,320 annually (CHF 3,777/month). In Italy, the cross-border worker declares CHF 60,000 (approximately €63,600) on form 730. Italian tax on €63,600 would be approximately €15,000. But the Italian tax credit recognizes approximately €7,900 (CHF 7,500) paid in Switzerland. Italian net refund: approximately €7,100. Total: CHF 45,320 net Swiss + CHF 7,500 Italian refund (tax credit) = substantial overall savings.
### Find a job and calculate net pay To find job positions in Ticino and neighboring cantons, consult the [job listings section of Frontaliere Ticino](nav:jobs). To calculate the approximate net salary considering Swiss federal/cantonal rates, tax at source, AVS/LPP contributions and Italian tax credit, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator). This tool integrates the New Cross-border Agreement in effect from January 1, 2024 and provides accurate estimates based on the applicable exemption (new vs. longtime cross-border workers).

## In a nutshell
- 79,121 border crossers in Ticino in Q2 2026, up quarterly - +0.64% vs Q1 2026 (+505 units); -0.57% on an annual basis - Distribution: 61.6% men, 38.4% women - Average age: 78% are between 30 and 59 years old
## Key facts
- **Number**: 79,121 border guards - When: 2026-Q2 (official BFS data) - Where: Canton Ticino, Switzerland - Who: Federal Statistical Office (BFS) - QoQ change: +505 units (+0.64%) vs Q1 - YoY variation: -457 units (-0.57%) vs Q2 2025 - Gender: Men 61.6%, Women 38.4%
The Federal Statistical Office (BFS) announced the number of border workers in the Canton of Ticino at the end of the second quarter of 2026: 79,121 people, up compared to the previous three months. The quarter therefore qualifies as an increase: the cyclical variation compared to Q1 2026 is positive by 505 units, equal to +0.64%. On an annual basis, however, the comparison with Q2 2025 shows a slight drop of 457 units (-0.57%), a sign of some volatility in the composition of the Ticino cross-border workforce.
### Quarterly change: the rebound from Q1
In the first quarter of 2026, the BFS statistic had recorded 78,616 border crossers. The recovery of 505 units in the following quarter represents a sign of stabilization after the winter months, when traditionally the number of members of the Federal Register of border workers tends to contract. The +0.64% growth, albeit modest, signals a positive trend in the labour market ### Reading the historical series: seasonal volatility and underlying trend
Looking at the eight quarters available from the BFS, the curve of the Ticino border crossers describes a trend that isfar from linear. In the first quarter of relevance (Q3 2024), the number reached 79,808, representing the maximum peak of the period examined. From there, the flow entered a phase of slight decline, reaching an all-time low in Q4 2025 with 78,698 border crossers. In the following quarter (Q1 2026), the contraction continued to 78,616, marking the point of greatest relative weakness. In Q2 2026 alone, the number rose to 79,121, while still remaining far from the 2024 high.
This trajectory suggests two fundamental considerations. First, seasonal volatility continues to weigh, with winter quarters (Q4, Q1) historically showing a contraction of a few hundred units. Second: net of seasonality, the underlying trend is oscillation around a range of 78,600-79,600 border crossers, without a clear upward or downward direction on multi-year scales. The BFS data therefore indicate an apparent stability, but with underlying dynamics of constant turnover.
### Master composition: the centre of gravity between the ages of 30 and 59

## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Implications for Payslip and Job Stability
For those who work or intend to look for a job beyond the Ticino border, the FSO figure of 79,121 cross-border workers is, first and foremost, a mirror of the health of the labour market. A stable number, despite slight quarterly fluctuations, signals that the use of cross-border labour remains a consolidated practice in the Ticino economic fabric. This allows those already working in Ticino to maintain reasonable job security, while for those seeking work the employment pool remains considered appealing. You can simulate the impact of a Ticino contract on your net salary using the [salary calculator](nav:calculator), which takes into account rates consistent with the cross-border market.
At the same time, the figures suggest that competition has not decreased. With the annual decline of -0.57% (457 fewer units compared to Q2 2025), it is possible that some positions previously held by cross-border workers have been reassigned to Swiss residents or citizens of other nationalities, especially in sectors where qualification is high (IT, finance, specialist healthcare). Those working in Ticino as cross-border workers must therefore pay attention to their positioning in the market: a career crystallised in a low-qualification position could prove fragile, while the push towards skills updating (languages, professional certifications, digital skills) remains strategic.
### Pension Planning: OASI, LPP and LAMal
The 79,121 cross-border workers registered in Q2 2026 are equally contributors to the Swiss social security systems. Every person working in Switzerland is obliged to pay contributions to the Old Age and Survivors' Insurance (OASI), to the occupational pension system (LPP) and to health insurance (LAMal). For cross-border workers, it is essential to understand how these payments integrate with tax and contribution obligations in Italy, thus avoiding pension gaps at retirement.
The FSO data do not provide a breakdown by sector or average income level, but the prevalence of cross-border workers in the 50-54 age bracket (almost 11,000 people) underlines the importance of adequately planning retirement. When a cross-border worker reaches 65 in Switzerland, they will have accumulated years of OASI and LPP contributions that will affect the pension. Timely communication with INPS, the Italian body, and monitoring of LPP plans with the Swiss employer remain crucial. For higher incomes, it is also advisable to check whether payments into the third pillar (Pillar 3a) and cantonal tax rebates are structured optimally to maximise supplementary pension provision.
### Concrete Actions: How to Move Now
1. Check your contract and contributions: Ensure that the Swiss employer correctly pays OASI and LPP contributions. Request a statement of contributions from the local OASI Compensation Office, to make sure there are no gaps.
2. **Update your professional profile**: With a slightly negative annual trend, job stability is not guaranteed. Invest in refresher courses and keep your CV competitive by browsing [job listings](nav:jobs) in growing sectors (specialist healthcare, green energy, fintech).
3. Plan your cross-border taxation: The FSO data do not break down by average income, but you know that your Swiss income is subject to withholding tax in Ticino and to declaration in Italy. Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) at least once a year to check the tax and pension impact on your payslip.
4. Monitor upcoming FSO data: The Federal Statistical Office publishes quarterly data regularly. If the next quarter signals a contraction greater than -1%, it will be time to reassess your contractual position or diversify your professional profile.
5. Consult a cross-border tax expert: For incomes exceeding CHF 150,000 per year, it is advisable to check whether deferral forms (second pillar, Pillar 3a, cantonal tax rebates) are structured correctly according to recent agreements between Switzerland and Italy.
Start today: access the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate your net income considering the gender composition data (61.6% men, 38.4% women) and by age bracket emerging from this FSO statistic. This will allow you to plan your pension and tax payments with awareness of the real employment trends in Ticino.

item.title: Border guesthouse 2026: plan with family and children
item.description: AVS 21 reform, new Frontier Agreement in force since 2024 and early retirement scenarios for those who work in Ticino with a family.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Unified AVS reference age at 65 years from 2024 - New Frontier Agreement in force from 1 January 2024 - Old frontier workers: exemption €7,500 until 2033 - New frontier workers: €10,000 exemption on tax at source
## Key facts - **What**: AVS pension advance possible up to 2 years before the reference age - When: AVS 21 reform in force since 2024, reference age 65 years - Where: Canton Ticino, for frontier workers with G permit - Who: AVS (Swiss first pillar), LPP (second pillar), INPS (Italy) - How it works: Withholding tax withheld only in Switzerland; Italy applies tax credit - Exemption for old frontier workers: €7,500, transitional regime 2024-2033 - New frontier tax exemption: €10,000 on tax at source - Regulatory reference: New Agreement signed on 23 December 2020, ratified by Law 83/2023
The reference age for the AVS annuity is set at 65 years for men and women from 2024, following the AVS 21 reform. Those who wish to advance their pension can do so up to two years beforehand, accepting a permanent reduction in their pension. For a border worker with family and children, the decision to anticipate retirement has direct effects on the second LPP pillar and coordination with the Italian INPS.
The AVS 21 reform also introduced a flexibility mechanism: it is possible to postpone the annuity beyond 65 years, obtaining a supplement calculated per year of Anticipating the AVS pension at 63 or 64 years old means accepting a permanent reduction in the first pillar pension. The penalty is more pronounced the further one moves away from the reference age of 65, and is also reflected in the amount of the LPP annuity, which is calculated on the accumulated old age at the time of exit. For a family with children still dependent or in the process of university studies, the economic framework changes significantly: early retirement reduces gross income but free time to devote to the family.
### Scenario comparison: anticipate or postpone Considering the Italian personal income tax rates in force — 23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, 43% over €50,000 — a frontier worker who anticipates retirement could be in a lower bracket, with theoretical tax savings. item.title: Canicola in the construction sites: Unia asks for mandatory breaks
item.description: Only 18% receive systematic breaks above 33°C. Out of 984 workers interviewed, 82% of construction sites ignore the protections provided. This is what the union is asking for.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Eight out of ten construction sites do not apply the mandatory breaks above 33°C - Unia asks for suspension of heavy work at 33 degrees and effective sanctions - Survey of 984 construction workers: only 18% have systematic time breaks - Ticino indicated as an example: suspension of work from 14:00 in heat waves
## Key facts - **What**: Unia survey on compliance with anti-heat measures in Swiss construction sites - When: July (interviews); results presented in Bern - Where: Switzerland (with positive mention of the Canton of Ticino) - Who: Unia trade union, 984 construction workers interviewed, Suva cited as technical source - Amount/Share: 18% with systematic breaks; 67% never; 15% sometimes; 32% with systematic cool place; 43% occasional; 25% without; 68% without early hours; 15% ill; +7% accident risk above 30°C - Proposal: Maximum threshold 33°C in the building works ordinance; breaks of 15 min/hour counted as work
In July, the Unia union interviewed 984 construction workers in all regions of Switzerland to verify the application of heat protection measures on construction sites. The results, presented in Bern, paint a critical picture: only 18% of respondents systematically benefit from 15-minute breaks per hour starting at 33 degrees. 67% state that such breaks are never granted, while 15% receive them "sometimes".
Even resting places remain a problem. Only a third (32%) of workers The Unia survey opens a trade union front that will also weigh in on Canton Ticino, where the construction sector permanently employs a significant share of Italian border workers. The data speak of a leopard-spot application of the protections already provided by law: 82% of Swiss shipyards do not regularly grant anti-heat breaks above 33°C and 25% of workers do not even have a cool place to stop.
For border crossers who cross the Brogeda, Chiasso or Gaggiolo crossings every morning towards the Lugano, Mendrisiotto or Bellinzonese shipyards, the question is not theoretical. Working at 14:00 with 35-39°C exposes you to an accident risk that, according to Suva data cited by Unia, grows by 7% above 30°C. 15% of respondents report personal or colleague illnesses: a share that, on an average site of ten workers, statistically corresponds to one or two episodes per season.
### What Unia is asking for and what it would actually change The union makes three precise requests. The first is the inclusion in the building works ordinance of a maximum threshold of 33°C: beyond this temperature, heavy outdoor physical work should be stopped, except for guaranteeing 15-minute breaks every hour in an air-conditioned place, counted as paid working hours.
The second request concerns controls: Unia asks Suva to strengthen inspections and, in case of incapacity, to entrust the task to the Cantons or
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). For a Ticino cross-border worker employed on a construction site, the first concrete step is to document. In the absence of a mandatory register of interruptions, it is advisable to keep a personal diary of the breaks granted or denied, the hours actually worked and the temperatures perceived. These notes become useful evidence in the event of illness, a wage dispute or a claim for compensation.
### Procedure in the event of illness on the construction site If a worker suffers heat-related illness, the chain of actions to follow is clear. First: immediately notify the site supervisor and, if the situation allows it, contact the emergency number. Second: be accompanied to a cool and shaded place, drink water, and stop all physical effort. Third: even if the illness seems to have passed, report it to your trusted doctor and keep any certificates, which are useful for any mandatory insurance coverage (UVG/LAA, KV/HIA for those who have opted for the Swiss system, daily allowance in the event of inability to work).
### Practical steps to enforce your rights Construction workers can contact the Unia union offices in Ticino for assistance on breaks not granted, unsuitable hours or the absence of rest areas. Reports can also be sent to Suva, which is responsible for occupational safety, and to SECO for matters relating to employment conditions. In the event of forced interruptions linked to bad weather, the existing compensation system does not currently cover heatwaves: the Unia proposal to extend compensation to heat is still awaiting passage in the Council of States.

Unia's pressure is not only union-based: if the 33°C threshold becomes mandatory, cross-border workers will also be able to count on written protection, no longer left to the discretion of the individual site supervisor.

item.title: Border tax credit 2026: common errors
item.description: Framework EC of 730, new Agreement in force since 2024 and transitional regime: the most frequent errors of border workers.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - New Frontier Agreement signed on 23/12/2020, in force from 1 January 2024 - Old frontier workers: exemption €7,500, transitional regime 2024–2033 - New frontier workers: deductible €10,000 - Withholding tax withheld only in Switzerland, credit in EC framework of 730
## Key facts - **What**: Tax credit to avoid double taxation on employee income in Switzerland - When: Income tax return 2026 (income 2025), second year of full operation of the new regime - Where: Canton of Ticino and the rest of Switzerland, declaration in Italy - Who: Frontier workers with G permit, INPS, Revenue Agency - Amount: Exemption €7,500 (old border guards), deductible €10,000 (new border guards) - Regulatory reference: Law 83 of 13/6/2023 (Italian ratification), Convention of 9 December 1976 - Declaratory framework: EC of model 730
The tax credit for border workers working in the Canton of Ticino — or more generally in Switzerland — is the mechanism by which Italy avoids double taxation on income produced overseas. From 1 January 2024, the new Agreement between Rome and Bern is in force, signed on 23 December 2020 and ratified by Italy with Law 83 of 13 June 2023. The 2026 tax return, relating to 2025 income, represents the second year of full operation of the updated regime.
### How credit works in the EC framework For frontier workers, the tax at source is withheld ## Practical analysis: where errors tend to concentrate
The experience of the last two filing campaigns — 2024 (for 2023 income, the launch year) and 2025 (for 2024 income, the first full year) — has brought to light a series of recurring critical issues. These are not data from a single study, but consolidated patterns that the Italian Revenue Agency and cross-border CAFs report in their operational communications.
### Mistake 1 — Confusing the tax credit with a refund Many taxpayers believe that Section CE generates a monetary credit from the Italian tax authority. In reality, the mechanism is different: the tax credit absorbs Italian IRPEF up to the amount of tax already paid in Switzerland. If the foreign tax exceeds the Italian one, the taxpayer does not receive anything extra; if the Italian tax is higher, they only pay the difference. Confusing this mechanism leads to entering incorrect amounts in the 730 form or to requesting unfounded refunds.
### Mistake 2 — Forgetting the Swiss payslip Swiss source deductions are not data that the Italian Revenue Agency receives automatically. They must be reported by the taxpayer based on the salary certificate issued by the Swiss employer. Omitting this entry — or entering an amount different from what was actually withheld — produces a tax credit inconsistent with the declared income, with possible anomaly flags.
### Mistake 3 — Failing to update the cross-border status Those who in 2025 switched from old to new cross-border status, or vice versa, must reconstruct the taxable base taking into account the different exemptions (€7,500 versus €10,000). The same applies to those who changed employer or canton: the source-tax rate varies, and Section CE must be populated with the correct data.
### Scenario comparison | Regime | Threshold/exemption | Declaration section | Error risk | |---|---|---|---| | Old cross-border (pre 17/7/2023) | €7,500 | CE with transitional period 2024–2033 | Medium | | New cross-border (post 17/7/2023) | €10,000 | Standard CE | High if the time cutoff is not known | | Commuter beyond 20 km | No special exemption | CE + double taxation check | High |
The table is not exhaustive: every situation must be assessed with your own CAF or advisor, but it captures the three most common scenarios among Canton Ticino workers. For details on the calculation, the [tax calculator for cross-border workers](nav:calculator) is useful, as it simulates the gross Swiss tax and the Italian credit.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ## What to do concretely: the step-by-step procedure
### Step 1 — Gather the documentation Before opening the 730 form, the cross-border worker must obtain: Swiss salary certificate (Lohnausweis), monthly pay slips, statement of AHV/AI/IPG contributions (5.3% borne by the employee) and AD/AC (1.1% with a cap of CHF 148,200), any LPP contributions (7–18% by age bracket, from age 25) and LAINF (0.7–1.5%). Without these documents, section CE cannot be filled out correctly.
### Step 2 — Verify the cross-border worker category Old or new cross-border worker — the distinction makes a difference: €7,500 exemption versus €10,000 allowance. The data must be cross-checked with the start date of the employment relationship in Switzerland.
### Step 3 — Fill out section CE In row CE3, the gross Swiss income must be indicated; in the following row, the foreign tax withheld. The software will calculate the credit due. ⚠️ A frequent mistake is to enter the net Swiss income instead of the gross: the credit would be understated.
### Step 4 — Submit the return and keep the documents The ordinary deadline for the 730 is 30 September (pre-filled form) or end of November (with CAF). It is essential to keep the Lohnausweis for at least five years, in case of an audit.
### Operational checklist - Lohnausweis 2025 received from the employer - Pay slips reconciled with the annual gross - AHV, LPP, LAINF contributions verified - Old/new cross-border worker status confirmed - Section CE completed with gross income (not net) - Foreign tax corresponding to the Lohnausweis
### When a preventive simulation is worthwhile For those who changed regime in 2025 or have multiple Swiss employers, it is worth running a simulation with the [net salary calculator](nav:payslip) before submitting. This helps detect category and rate errors.
For taxpayers who wish to verify the impact of pension contributions — AHV, LPP and any third pillar 3a — the dedicated [pillar 3a](nav:pillar3) page is also available. On the insurance side, the [LAMal guide for cross-border workers](nav:health) clarifies the healthcare coverage options.
To avoid the most common pitfalls of section CE and obtain an up-to-date 2026 simulation, use the [salary calculator for cross-border workers](nav:calculator) before submitting the return.

item.title: 2026 tax credit: calculation for family with children
item.description: Frontier workers with children: CE framework of 730, deductible €10,000 new and €7,500 old. Calculation of tax credit, withholding tax withheld in Switzerland, return deadlines 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Box CE of 730: tax credit from Swiss withholdings CHF - 2026 exemption: €10,000 new cross-border workers, €7,500 old until 2033 - New Agreement effective January 1, 2024, avoids double taxation
## Key facts - **What**: Tax credit for recovery of source tax withheld only in Switzerland - When: 2026 tax return (year 2025); Agreement effective 1/1/2024 - Where: Box CE, Italian 730 form at the Revenue Agency - Who: Cross-border workers with Permit G (dependent work in Ticino/Switzerland) - Amount: €10,000 exemption for new, €7,500 exemption for old (transitional 2024-2033) - Source tax: Withheld ONLY in Switzerland (5.3% AVS/AI/IPG employee) - Bilateral convention: December 9, 1976 Italy-Switzerland (avoids double taxation)
In 2026, cross-border workers with children working in Ticino will continue to benefit from the tax credit for source taxes withheld in Switzerland. The system works as follows: Switzerland withholds income tax on work income according to its rates (AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% for employees, plus any insurance contributions LAINF 0.7–1.5% and cantonal); Italy, applying the bilateral convention of December 9, 1976 and the New Cross-border Agreement effective January 1, 2024, recognizes the tax credit in the 730 form, box CE, thus avoiding double taxation. The Italian return accounts for differentiated exemptions: €10,000 for cross-border workers who became such after July 17, 2023 (new), €7,500 for old cross-border workers with transitional regime until 2033.
The practical consequence is that, within the limits of the exemption, the amount paid in Switzerland is deducted from the Italian taxable income, reducing overall tax pressure. For families with children, the advantage increases thanks to family allowances and deductions for family dependents, which Italy recognizes in the return. Using the [salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator), you can simulate the impact of the exemption on your net income.
### How the New Agreement changed the framework The New Cross-border Agreement, signed December 23, 2020 and effective January 1, 2024 (ratified in Italy with Law 83 of June 13, 2023), introduced a clear differentiation between old and new cross-border workers. The old ones (already such before July 17, 2023) benefit from a €7,500 exemption in transitional regime until 2033; the new ones have a permanent €10,000 flat exemption. This means that the first euro of income beyond the exemption is subject to ordinary Italian tax according to IRPEF rates (23% up to €28,000, 35% up to €50,000, 43% above €50,000). Before January 2024, the mechanism was less defined; the Agreement has standardized and clarified the procedure, facilitating tax planning for families. In concrete terms, how does the calculation of the tax credit for a border family with children in 2026 work?
### Scenario: border crossing with two children A border worker with two children, employed in Ticino with annual gross income, suffers Swiss withholdings from Switzerland (5.3% for AVS/AI/IPG employee, plus any LAINF 0.7–1.5% and administrative/cantonal contributions). The Swiss net amount is reduced by about 6-8% due to these withholdings. At the time of the Italian declaration, the taxpayer enters the total amount of withholdings in the EC framework and, thanks to the deductible of €7,500 (if old border) or €10,000 (if new), recovers the tax credit on part of the taxable amount.
In this way, the taxpayer does not suffer double taxation: Switzerland withholds a percentage, Italy recognizes the credit and applies its personal income tax rates only on income that exceeds the deductible. For a family with two children, the additional deductions (universal one-off checks, historically dependant deductions) further reduce the Italian net tax. Coordination with INPS ensures that family allowances are recognised as long as the total income of the family remains within the established limits.
### Difference Between Old Regime and New Agreement Before 1 January 2024, frontier workers were treated with less transparency about deductibles. The New Agreement has standardized the mechanism: a clear line between ### Step-by-step procedure: completing section CE in form 730 1. **Collect documents**: receive from the Swiss employer (or from the competent canton through the municipal tax administration) the certification of source taxes withheld during the year. Also keep December payslips or cantonal tax certificates, as well as any receipts for contributions paid to INPS for pension contributions paid in duplicate. 2. Enter data in section CE: in the Italian 730 form, section "Foreign employment income", enter the gross amount earned in Switzerland (in CHF) and the total amount of source tax withheld, converted to EUR at the exchange rate of the fiscal year-end date. 3. Declare children: in the section "Dependent family members" or "Universal family allowances", list the children with their data (tax ID, date of birth, any personal income). The Revenue Agency will automatically apply deductions if the family income falls within the regulatory limits. 4. Verify the threshold: make sure you have clearly noted whether you are an old cross-border worker (exemption €7,500) or new (threshold €10,000). This determines which portion of income is taxable in Italy and which remains covered by the Swiss tax credit. 5. File the 730: submit the return through a CAF (Tax Assistance Center), a tax advisor, or online on the Revenue Agency portal by the ordinary deadline.
### Deadlines and timelines The deadlines for filing the 730 return follow the standard Italian calendar (generally May-June for the paper form, July for the electronic version). It is advisable to complete the compilation by the ordinary deadline to avoid penalties and quickly receive the tax credit.
### Checklist for cross-border families with children - ☐ Collect source tax certificates from Switzerland (amounts in CHF) - ☐ Verify whether you are old cross-border workers (before 17/7/2023) or new (from 17/7/2023 onwards) - ☐ Convert CHF amounts to EUR (ECB exchange rate at year-end) - ☐ Enter gross amounts and withholdings in section CE of form 730 - ☐ List children and dependent family members with tax ID, date of birth, personal income - ☐ Verify that deductions for children and dependent family members are applied - ☐ Check that the tax credit covers at least the applicable threshold (€7,500 or €10,000)

item.title: Border payroll 2026 over 20 km: complete guide
item.description: Swiss paycheck 2026 for border workers over 20 km: withholdings, contributions and real net after the New Agreement in force from 1 January 2024.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Tax at source only in Switzerland for Italian border workers - New Agreement signed on 23/12/2020, effective from 1 January 2024 - Old border guards: exemption €7,500; new: deductible €10,000 - Italy-Switzerland double taxation agreement of 9 December 1976
## Key facts - **What**: Withholding tax withheld exclusively in Switzerland on the income from work of border workers - When: Regime in force from 1 January 2024 (New Agreement signed on 23 December 2020) - Where: Canton of Ticino and the rest of Switzerland; avoidance of double taxation in Italy by means of a tax credit (EC framework of 730) - Who: AFC/ESTV at the federal level and cantonal administrations of contributions for the tax part; INPS for social security - Amount: Old frontier workers exemption €7,500 (transitional regime 2024–2033), new frontier workers exemption €10,000 - When: Italian ratification with Law 83 of 13 June 2023 - Who: SECO, SEM, SUVA among the reference bodies; INPS and Agenzia delle Entrate on the Italian side
From 1 January 2024, the paycheck of the Ticino border worker who works more than 20 km from the border follows completely new tax rules. The New Agreement between Italy and Switzerland, signed in Rome on 23 December 2020 and ratified by Italy with Law 83 of 13 June 2023, redesigned the taxation of frontier workers. Switzerland is not a member of the EU or the EEA: the bilateral relationship is still based on the Convention against Doubles The rates that appear on the paycheck of a Ticino border worker in 2026 are divided into three blocks: social contributions, taxes and insurance. Understanding the difference is essential to reading the slip.
### Swiss social contributions on payroll The AVS/AI/IPG part is equal to 5.3% borne by the employee (out of a total of 10.6% with AVS 2024 reform, half of which is borne by the worker). To this is added the AD (unemployment insurance) contribution of 1.1%, taken up to the ceiling of CHF 148,200. Beyond that threshold, the AC solidarity contribution is triggered, equal to 1% on high incomes. The LAINF premium (accident insurance) varies between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the business risk. The LPP occupational pension, compulsory from the age of 25 for incomes above the coordination threshold, provides for rates between 7% and 18% depending on the age group.
### Italian personal income tax and tax credit For those who are over 20 km from the border and fall under the ordinary regime (not exempt), the Italian personal income tax is applied in three stages: 23% up to €28,000, 35% between €28,001 and €50,000, 43% over €50,000. Double taxation is avoided with the tax credit in the EC framework of model 730: the worker declares foreign income and discharges the tax already paid in Switzerland.
### Scenario comparison: old vs. new border crossers A border crossing already in place before 17 July 2023 enjoys the transitional regime 2024–2033
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). To navigate the 2026 payslip of a cross-border commuter beyond 20 km, it helps to follow a precise path: first identify the deductions, then calculate the real net pay, and finally plan the tax return in Italy.
### 2026 payslip operational checklist 1. Check the deductions on the pay slip. Make sure the following appear: withholding tax (cantonal and communal rate), OASI/DI/IC 5.3%, UI 1.1% (up to CHF 148,200), SUI 1% above the threshold, LAA 0.7–1.5%, LPP 7–18% by age bracket. If any of these items is missing, ask your employer for clarification.
2. Check the allowance or exemption. Old cross-border commuters have an exemption of up to €7,500, new ones up to €10,000. The amount must be compared with the gross annual income converted into euros at the reference exchange rate.
**3. Check LAMal health insurance.** G permit holders can choose between Swiss LAMal (with the right of option) and an equivalent Italian insurance, with standard deductibles between CHF 300 and CHF 2,500 for adults. Do not confuse LAMal with the so-called 'health tax': it is an insurance, not a tax.
4. Keep your pay slips and salary certificate. They are needed for the income tax return in Italy, where the foreign income must be reported in section RC of the 730 form and the foreign tax in section CE as a tax credit.
5. 2026 deadlines. The ordinary deadline for the 730 is the end of September. Repayments are calculated annually; the foreign income tax return is mandatory even when the net Italian tax is zero.
